SURG-017.population: 117 BR/LA PDAC patients resected after neoadjuvant therapy.
SURG-017.finding: Perioperative morbidity/mortality similar between groups. Median OS SMV/PV resection vs preservation 16.0 vs 22.0 mo (p=0.965); DFS 10.0 vs 12.0 mo (p=0.843). Within resections, histologic venous invasion -> much shorter OS (8.3 vs 24.0 mo, p<0.0001) and DFS (5.0 vs 17.0 mo, p=0.0002). R0 > R1 for OS/DFS. On multivariable analysis R1 and histologic SMV/PV invasion independently predicted worse OS.
SURG-017.effect: Venous invasion ~3x shorter OS; resection per se not prognostic.

glosses.pancreas-neck: Series of 117 patients resected after neoadjuvant therapy showing vein resection itself did not shorten survival but cancer in the vein wall did.
glosses.smv-portal-vein: Series of 117 patients resected after neoadjuvant therapy showing vein resection itself did not shorten survival but cancer in the vein wall did.
glosses.vessel-contact: A 117-patient post-chemotherapy series in which vein resection itself did not change survival but histologic venous invasion shortened it three-fold.
glosses.vascular-resection: A series of 117 patients resected after chemotherapy in which vein resection itself did not affect survival but vein-wall invasion did.

SURG-018.citation: Barrak D, Villano AM, Villafane-Ferriol N, Stockton LG, Hill MV, Deng M, et al. Total neoadjuvant therapy for pancreatic adenocarcinoma increases probability for a complete pathologic response. Eur J Surg Oncol. 2022;48(6):1356-1361.
SURG-018.clinical_status: TNT increasingly used (US); pCR not a cure endpoint
SURG-018.design: Retrospective NCDB cohort; multivariable logistic (pCR) + survival.
SURG-018.population: 5402 patients with LA/borderline PDAC who received neoadjuvant therapy then resection; US National Cancer Database 2006-2016.
SURG-018.finding: pCR (down-stage to pathologic stage 0) in 177 (3.3%). Of these, 57 had chemo, 41 chemoradiation, 79 TNT. TNT more likely to confer pCR than chemoradiation (OR 1.67, 1.13-2.46, p=0.0103) or chemo (OR 2.61, 1.83-3.71, p<0.0001). pCR -> median OS 64.9 vs 21.6 mo without pCR (p<0.0001).
SURG-018.effect: pCR rare (3.3%) but ~3x longer median OS; TNT raises pCR odds.
SURG-018.limitations: Administrative coding; no central path review; survivor/immortal-time considerations.
SURG-018.interpretation: Large observational; association of pCR with survival, confounded by responder biology.

glosses.microscopic-disease: A US database analysis showing pathologic complete response in 3.3% of neoadjuvant-treated patients, associated with longer but not guaranteed survival.
glosses.ctdna: A national database study in which complete pathologic response occurred in 3.3% and was followed by recurrence in some patients despite long median survival.
glosses.pathology-report: A national database study in which complete pathologic response occurred in 3.3% and carried a median survival of 64.9 months.

SURG-019.citation: Gemenetzis G, Groot VP, Blair AB, Laheru DA, Zheng L, Narang AK, et al. Survival in Locally Advanced Pancreatic Cancer After Neoadjuvant Therapy and Surgical Resection. Ann Surg. 2019;270(2):340-347.
SURG-019.clinical_status: selective conversion surgery practiced (US high-volume centres)
SURG-019.design: Prospective-registry retrospective cohort; resected vs non-resected; time-matched analysis.
SURG-019.population: 415 LAPC patients, pancreatic multidisciplinary clinic (Johns Hopkins), 2013-2017.
SURG-019.finding: 84/415 (20%) underwent resection after median 5 mo neoadjuvant therapy. FOLFIRINOX-based therapy and SBRT correlated with higher resection probability (p=0.006). Resected patients had smaller tumours and lower CA19-9. Median OS resected 35.3 vs non-resected 16.3 mo (p<0.001); remained significant when non-resected matched for neoadjuvant duration (19.9 mo, p<0.001).
SURG-019.effect: Resection after conversion ~2x median OS vs matched non-resected.
SURG-019.limitations: Single high-volume centre; selection; no randomization.
SURG-019.interpretation: Observational with time-matching to mitigate immortal-time bias; still selection-limited.

glosses.resectability-categories: A 415-patient locally advanced cohort in which 20% reached resection after chemotherapy, with resected patients living about twice as long as matched non-resected patients.
glosses.sma: Johns Hopkins series of 415 locally advanced cancers in which 20% reached resection after chemotherapy, with longer survival in those resected.
glosses.treatment-sequencing: Among 415 patients with locally advanced disease at one center, 20% were resected after chemotherapy and lived a median of 35.3 months versus 16.3 months for those not resected, a selected comparison.

SURG-020.citation: Gemenetzis G, Blair AB, Nagai M, Groot VP, Ding D, Fishman EK, et al. Anatomic Criteria Determine Resectability in Locally Advanced Pancreatic Cancer. Ann Surg Oncol. 2022;29(1):401-414.
SURG-020.design: Retrospective cohort; anatomic stratification vs resection and survival.
SURG-020.population: Same 415 LAPC patients (2013-2018), prospectively stratified LAPC-1/2/3 by regional vessel involvement.
SURG-020.finding: Resection rate 49% (LAPC-1), 32% (LAPC-2), 11% (LAPC-3) (p<0.001). Resected patients with LAPC-score improvement at exploration had median OS 60.7 vs 29.8 mo (no change/progression) (p=0.006). Overall resected median OS 35.3 mo.
SURG-020.effect: Anatomic score strongly predicts resectability; radiographic improvement doubles OS among resected.

glosses.resectability-categories: A companion study showing an anatomic vessel-involvement score predicts the chance of eventual resection in locally advanced disease.
glosses.sma: Companion analysis showing an anatomic vessel-involvement score predicted resection rates of 49%, 32% and 11% in locally advanced disease.
glosses.celiac-hepatic-arteries: Companion analysis showing an anatomic vessel-involvement score predicted resection rates of 49%, 32% and 11% in locally advanced disease.
glosses.vessel-contact: A non-counting lead in which an anatomic score for locally advanced tumors predicted resection rates of 49%, 32% and 11%.
glosses.restaging: A non-counting lead in which locally advanced tumors whose anatomic score improved on imaging had twice the median survival after resection.

SURG-021.citation: Hank T, Klaiber U, Hinz U, Schutte D, Leonhardt CS, Bergmann F, et al. Oncological Outcome of Conversion Surgery After Preoperative Chemotherapy for Metastatic Pancreatic Cancer. Ann Surg. 2023;277(5):e1089-e1098.
SURG-021.design: Retrospective cohort; resection vs exploration-only; univariable/multivariable survival.
SURG-021.population: 173 metastatic PDAC patients explored after preoperative chemotherapy (Heidelberg, 2006-2019).
SURG-021.finding: Among 93 resected: 45 had complete pathologic response of metastases (ypM0), 48 residual (ypM1). OS: ypM0 25.5 mo, ypM1 10.7 mo, no resection 8.1 mo (p<0.001). Adjuvant chemo improved survival in resected (29.0 vs 14.8 mo, p=0.024) and in ypM0 (29.1 vs 19.2 mo, p=0.047). Conversion surgery, CA19-9 and timing were independent prognostic markers.
SURG-021.effect: ypM0 resection ~3x OS vs no resection; adjuvant adds further benefit.
SURG-021.interpretation: Observational; strong selection by exceptional response (confounding by indication).

glosses.liver: Heidelberg series showing surgery for metastatic disease helped only patients whose metastases had been pathologically cleared by chemotherapy.

SURG-022.citation: Lee JW, Stone ML, Porrett PM, Thomas SK, Komar CA, Li JH, et al. Hepatocytes direct the formation of a pro-metastatic niche in the liver. Nature. 2019;567(7747):249-252.
SURG-022.design: Genetic ablation/blockade of IL-6/STAT3/SAA in hepatocytes + patient correlation.
SURG-022.population: Mouse PDAC (and colorectal) models; patient serum/liver samples.
SURG-022.n: Mouse cohorts; patient samples (liver-met vs not).
SURG-022.finding: Early in pancreatic tumorigenesis, hepatocytes activate STAT3 and produce serum amyloid A1/A2 (SAA), coordinating myeloid-cell accumulation and fibrosis that render the liver susceptible to seeding/outgrowth. Hepatocyte STAT3/SAA depends on IL-6 released by non-malignant cells. Genetic ablation or blockade of IL-6/STAT3/SAA prevents the pro-metastatic niche and inhibits liver metastasis. SAA overexpression by hepatocytes also seen in pancreatic/colorectal cancer patients with liver metastases; circulating SAA elevated in advanced disease.
SURG-022.effect: IL-6/STAT3/SAA blockade -> prevented niche and reduced liver metastasis (categorical).
SURG-022.limitations: Mouse mechanism; human data observational; IL-6/STAT3 blockade not validated clinically for this indication.
SURG-022.interpretation: Loss-of-function + rescue in mice; human correlation -> strong mechanistic + translational link.

glosses.microscopic-disease: A mouse study showing liver cells respond to tumor-driven interleukin-6 by creating a pro-metastatic niche.
glosses.recurrence-meaning: A mouse study showing liver cells respond to tumor-driven interleukin-6 by creating a pro-metastatic niche.
glosses.liver: Mouse study showing IL-6-driven hepatocyte signaling creates a pro-metastatic niche in the liver.
glosses.liver-niche: A mouse and human study showing hepatocytes driven by interleukin-6 produce serum amyloid A that prepares the liver, with blockade preventing metastasis.
glosses.liver-lesions: A mouse study in which liver cells, signalled by IL-6, produced inflammatory proteins that made the liver receptive to metastasis.

SURG-023.citation: Nielsen SR, Quaranta V, Linford A, Emeagi P, Rainer C, Santos A, et al. Macrophage-secreted granulin supports pancreatic cancer metastasis by inducing liver fibrosis. Nat Cell Biol. 2016;18(5):549-60.
SURG-023.design: Perturbation (MAM recruitment disruption; granulin genetic depletion) + patient correlation.
SURG-023.population: Mouse PDAC liver-metastasis models; PDAC patient monocytes/hepatic macrophages.
SURG-023.finding: PDAC liver metastasis depends on early recruitment of granulin-secreting inflammatory monocytes. MAM granulin activates resident hepatic stellate cells into myofibroblasts secreting periostin -> fibrotic microenvironment sustaining metastatic growth. Disrupting MAM recruitment or depleting granulin reduced stellate activation and liver metastasis. PDAC patient circulating monocytes and hepatic MAMs express high granulin.
SURG-023.interpretation: Genetic/pharmacologic perturbation in vivo supports causal niche role.

glosses.recurrence-meaning: A mouse study showing macrophage-secreted granulin drives liver fibrosis that supports metastatic growth.
glosses.liver: Mouse study showing macrophage-derived granulin drives liver fibrosis that sustains pancreatic cancer metastases.
glosses.myeloid-cells: A mouse and patient-sample study showing that granulin secreted by liver macrophages activates hepatic stellate cells into a fibrotic niche that sustains pancreatic cancer metastasis.
glosses.liver-niche: A mouse and human study showing macrophage-secreted granulin activates hepatic stellate cells into a periostin-rich fibrotic niche that sustains metastasis.

SURG-024.citation: Quaranta V, Rainer C, Nielsen SR, Raymant ML, Ahmed MS, Engle DD, et al. Macrophage-Derived Granulin Drives Resistance to Immune Checkpoint Inhibition in Metastatic Pancreatic Cancer. Cancer Res. 2018;78(15):4253-4269.
SURG-024.design: Genetic granulin depletion + anti-PD-1; CD8 T-cell infiltration and metastatic burden.
SURG-024.finding: Macrophage-derived granulin (induced by CSF-1) causes CD8+ T-cell exclusion in metastatic livers via a fibrotic stroma. Metastatic PDAC is largely resistant to anti-PD-1; granulin depletion reduced fibrosis, allowed T-cell entry, and PD-1 blockade then restored anti-tumour immunity and dramatically decreased metastatic burden.
SURG-024.effect: Granulin depletion converts anti-PD-1-resistant metastases to responsive (categorical).
SURG-024.limitations: Preclinical; no human ICI-combination outcome data.
SURG-024.interpretation: Combination perturbation supports causal link niche fibrosis -> immune exclusion -> ICI resistance.

glosses.recurrence-meaning: A mouse study showing macrophage-derived granulin excludes T cells from liver metastases and causes checkpoint-inhibitor resistance.
glosses.liver: Mouse study showing granulin-driven fibrosis excludes T cells from liver metastases and blocks checkpoint immunotherapy.
glosses.myeloid-cells: A mouse study showing the same macrophage granulin program excludes CD8 T cells from liver metastases and causes resistance to PD-1 blockade, reversed when granulin is removed.
glosses.liver-niche: A mouse study showing the same granulin-driven liver fibrosis excludes CD8 T cells and causes PD-1 blockade resistance, reversed by depleting granulin.

SURG-025.citation: Aiello NM, Maddipati R, Norgard RJ, Balli D, Li J, Yuan S, et al. EMT Subtype Influences Epithelial Plasticity and Mode of Cell Migration. Dev Cell. 2018;45(6):681-695.e4.
SURG-025.design: In vivo lineage tracing of EMT program type; migration-mode assays.
SURG-025.population: Lineage-labeled mouse PDAC in vivo; breast/colorectal cell lines.
SURG-025.n: Mouse models + multiple carcinoma cell lines.
SURG-025.finding: Most PDAC tumours lose epithelial phenotype via an ALTERNATIVE program involving internalization/re-localization of epithelial proteins (not transcriptional repression), yielding a 'partial EMT'. Partial-EMT cells migrate as CLUSTERS (collective migration) and form circulating tumour-cell clusters, contrasting with single-cell migration of classical EMT. Program conserved across breast/colorectal lines.
SURG-025.effect: Partial EMT -> collective/cluster migration and CTC clusters (qualitative mechanism).
SURG-025.interpretation: In vivo lineage tracing distinguishes competing EMT mechanisms.

SURG-026.citation: Maddipati R, Stanger BZ. Pancreatic Cancer Metastases Harbor Evidence of Polyclonality. Cancer Discov. 2015;5(10):1086-97.
SURG-026.design: Multicolor lineage tracing of clonal composition across primary, precursors, and metastases.
SURG-026.finding: Precursor lesions show marked clonal heterogeneity that DECREASES during premalignant progression. A significant fraction of metastases are POLYCLONALLY seeded by distinct subclones. Clonality during metastatic growth (monoclonal vs polyclonal expansion) DIFFERS by site of metastatic invasion; heterotypic interactions between subpopulations contribute to metastatic progression.
SURG-026.effect: Polyclonal seeding common; clonality is organ-dependent (qualitative).
SURG-026.limitations: Mouse model; no human genomic confirmation here (cf. Campbell organ-specific branches).
SURG-026.interpretation: In vivo lineage tracing supports polyclonal seeding causally (mouse).

glosses.liver-niche: A multicolor lineage-tracing mouse study showing a substantial share of metastases are seeded by more than one subclone, with clonality differing by organ.
glosses.genome-evolution: A mouse lineage study showing many metastases are seeded by more than one subclone.

SUPP-001.citation: Forsmark CE, Tang G, Xu H, Tuft M, Hughes SJ, Yadav D. The use of pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy in patients with a diagnosis of chronic pancreatitis and pancreatic cancer in the US is infrequent and inconsistent. Aliment Pharmacol Ther. 2020;51(10):958-967.
SUPP-001.clinical_status: Pancrelipase products FDA-approved for exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (US); guideline-recommended practice to test/treat after pancreatic surgery; checked 2026-10-08
SUPP-001.design: Retrospective administrative-claims cohort; pharmacy claims for PERT (NDC codes), testing codes for exocrine insufficiency; multivariable logistic regression for predictors of use and of adequate dose (defined >=120,000 USP lipase units/day)
SUPP-001.population: US commercially insured population (IQVIA PharMetrics claims, 48.67 million enrollees, 2001-2013); 32,461 individuals with a pancreatic cancer claim (ICD-9 157.x) and 37,061 with chronic pancreatitis
SUPP-001.time_frame: Claims 2001-2013; median enrollment after pancreatic cancer diagnosis 10 months
SUPP-001.finding: Pancreatic cancer cohort: 7,125/32,461 (21.9%) ever filled PERT; 1,800 (5.5% of all; 27.5% of PERT users) received >=120,000 USP units/day; only 1.9% had any test for exocrine insufficiency; when tests were done (both cohorts) fecal chymotrypsin 53%, fecal fat 38%, fecal elastase 9%. Strongest predictors of any PERT use in pancreatic cancer: pancreatic surgery OR 3.25 (95% CI 3.05-3.46), any exocrine-insufficiency test OR 2.94 (2.48-3.48), seeing a GI physician OR 1.88 (1.72-2.06). Among PERT users overall, 30% used <40,000 units/day and 57% <80,000 units/day. Proportions were stable over 2001-2013 (Results text; Tables 1-6 in manuscript).
SUPP-001.effect: Descriptive proportions and adjusted ORs as above
SUPP-001.limitations: No clinical outcomes; 2001-2013 era (pre-modern guidelines); commercially insured only; cannot distinguish resected vs advanced beyond surgery codes
SUPP-001.interpretation: Descriptive population-level utilization; identifies under-testing and under-dosing but cannot show outcomes of PERT

glosses.digestion-enzymes: US insurance-claims data from 2001-2013 showed most people with pancreatic cancer were never tested for enzyme insufficiency and few received adequately dosed enzymes.
glosses.acinar-cells: US claims analysis showing only 22% of pancreatic cancer patients ever fill an enzyme prescription and 2% are tested for insufficiency.
glosses.enzyme-replacement: A US claims study of 32,461 people with pancreatic cancer from 2001 to 2013 showing that about one in five ever filled an enzyme prescription and one in fifty was tested.

SUPP-002.citation: Seiler CM, Izbicki J, Varga-Szabó L, Czakó L, Fiók J, Sperti C, et al. Randomised clinical trial: a 1-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of pancreatin 25 000 Ph. Eur. minimicrospheres (Creon 25000 MMS) for pancreatic exocrine insufficiency after pancreatic surgery, with a 1-year open-label extension. Aliment Pharmacol Ther. 2013;37(7):691-702.
SUPP-002.clinical_status: Pancrelipase FDA-approved for exocrine pancreatic insufficiency incl. after pancreatectomy (US label: starting 500-1,000 lipase units/kg/meal for chronic pancreatitis or pancreatectomy; do not exceed 2,500 units/kg/meal or 10,000 units/kg/day; DailyMed effective 2024-02-28); checked 2026-10-08
SUPP-002.design: Multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group RCT (1 week) with 1-year open-label extension; primary endpoint change in CFA (72-h fecal fat with standardized diet)
SUPP-002.population: Adults with exocrine insufficiency (coefficient of fat absorption, CFA <80%) after pancreatic resection (50% Whipple/PPPD or equivalent, 22% duodenum-preserving head resection, 7% total pancreatectomy; cancer and chronic pancreatitis); mean time since surgery ~53 months
SUPP-002.finding: Least-squares mean CFA change: pancreatin +21.4% (95% CI 13.7-29.2) vs placebo -4.2% (-12.8 to 4.5); difference 25.6% (13.9-37.3), P<0.001. Open-label: mean CFA rose from 53.6+/-20.6% at baseline to 78.4+/-20.7% at 1 year (P<0.001). Treatment-emergent AEs 37.5% pancreatin vs 26.9% placebo (flatulence 12.5% vs 7.7%). Anatomy effect: of patients whose operations alter motility/site of enzyme release (total pancreatectomy, Whipple or equivalent, duodenum-preserving head resection) only 7/26 (27%) reached on-treatment CFA >85%, versus a higher proportion after operations less likely to affect motility (Results text; Tables 1-5).
SUPP-002.limitations: Small n; mixed benign/malignant; only ~27% of Whipple-type patients normalized fat absorption, so the trial also shows the ceiling of PERT after reconstruction
SUPP-002.interpretation: Randomized, blinded: establishes that high-dose enteric-coated enzymes raise fat absorption after pancreatic surgery (causal, human interventional)

glosses.digestion-enzymes: A placebo-controlled trial after pancreatic surgery found enzyme capsules raised fat absorption by about 26 points but normalized it in only 27% of Whipple-type patients.
glosses.nutrition: A placebo-controlled trial found enzyme capsules raised fat absorption after surgery but normalized it in only 27% of Whipple-type patients.
glosses.life-after-whipple: A placebo-controlled trial found enzyme capsules raised fat absorption after surgery but normalized it in only 27% of Whipple-type patients.
glosses.acinar-cells: Placebo-controlled trial showing enzyme capsules raised fat absorption by 25 percentage points after pancreatic surgery, with limited normalization after Whipple-type operations.
glosses.duodenum: Placebo-controlled trial showing enzyme capsules raised fat absorption by 25 percentage points after pancreatic surgery, with limited normalization after Whipple-type operations.
glosses.stomach: Placebo-controlled trial showing enzyme capsules raised fat absorption by 25 percentage points after pancreatic surgery, with limited normalization after Whipple-type operations.
glosses.whipple: A placebo-controlled trial in which enzyme capsules raised fat absorption after pancreatic surgery but normalized it in only 27% of Whipple-type patients.
glosses.total-pancreatectomy: A placebo-controlled enzyme trial after pancreatic surgery, including total pancreatectomy, showing improved but rarely normal fat absorption.
glosses.enzyme-replacement: A double-blind trial of 58 people with fat malabsorption after pancreatic surgery in which high-dose pancrelipase raised fat absorption by about 26 percentage points, with incomplete normalization after Whipple-type operations.

SUPP-003.citation: Choi Y, Oh DY, Kim TY, Lee KH, Han SW, Im SA, Kim TY, Bang YJ. Skeletal Muscle Depletion Predicts the Prognosis of Patients with Advanced Pancreatic Cancer Undergoing Palliative Chemotherapy, Independent of Body Mass Index. PLoS One. 2015;10(10):e0139749.
SUPP-003.clinical_status: Not applicable (prognostic observation); CT body-composition analysis is research-grade, not standard of care; checked 2026-10-08
SUPP-003.design: Retrospective cohort; CT-based L3 skeletal muscle index (SMI) at diagnosis and at progression; sex-specific sarcopenia cut-offs from ROC (<42.2 cm2/m2 men, <33.9 women); Cox models for overall survival
SUPP-003.population: 484 consecutive patients with histologically confirmed advanced pancreatic cancer (80.2% metastatic) receiving palliative chemotherapy (90.7% gemcitabine-based) at Seoul National University Hospital, 2003-2012
SUPP-003.time_frame: Diagnosis 2003-2012; median follow-up 11.0 months; SMI measured at diagnosis and at progression
SUPP-003.finding: Sarcopenia at diagnosis in 103/484 (21.3%). SMI decreased (>2 cm2/m2) in 60.9% of men and 40.6% of women during first-line chemotherapy; BMI decreased in 37.3%. Median OS 8.4 months (95% CI 7.6-9.2). Multivariable: sarcopenia HR 1.72 (95% CI 1.30-2.28, P<0.001); decreased BMI HR 1.45 (1.15-1.84, P=0.002); decreased SMI HR 1.39 (1.11-1.74, P=0.004). Men with sarcopenia: median OS 6.1 vs 9.4 months. Among patients whose BMI was maintained, SMI loss still predicted worse OS (HR 1.50, P=0.002), whereas BMI change did not matter when SMI was maintained (P=0.75) (Tables 3-4, Fig 3-4).
SUPP-003.effect: Adjusted HR for death: sarcopenia 1.72; muscle loss during chemo 1.39
SUPP-003.limitations: Single centre, retrospective; ROC-derived cut-offs (optimistic); CT timing varied; mostly gemcitabine era
SUPP-003.interpretation: Prognostic association in a large cohort; muscle loss is independent of weight (dissociation of scale from body-composition change)

glosses.weight-loss-cachexia: A Korean cohort of 484 people on palliative chemotherapy found muscle loss on CT predicted shorter survival even when weight was maintained.
glosses.fatigue: A Korean cohort found muscle loss during first-line chemotherapy in 61% of men and 41% of women.
glosses.nutrition: A Korean cohort found muscle loss during chemotherapy in many patients whose weight was stable.
glosses.growth-factor-support: A retrospective cohort of 484 people on palliative chemotherapy in which loss of skeletal muscle predicted shorter survival independently of body-mass index.
glosses.cachexia-treatments: A retrospective cohort of 484 people on palliative chemotherapy in which loss of skeletal muscle predicted shorter survival independently of body-mass index.
glosses.cachexia-research: A 484-patient cohort showing that muscle loss during chemotherapy for advanced pancreatic cancer predicts shorter survival independently of body weight.

SUPP-004.citation: Bergenfeldt H, Fagher K, Williamsson C, Andersson B. New-onset diabetes after distal pancreatectomy-findings from a national cohort study. Ann Hepatobiliary Pancreat Surg. 2026;30(3):367-373.
SUPP-004.clinical_status: Not applicable (natural history after surgery); checked 2026-10-08
SUPP-004.design: Population-based registry cohort; competing-risk (Fine-Gray) regression for new-onset diabetes (NODM) with death as competing event
SUPP-004.population: 1,034 patients without pre-existing diabetes undergoing distal pancreatectomy in Sweden 2010-2020 (Swedish National Pancreatic and Periampullary Cancer Registry cross-linked to the National Diabetes Register); 35% malignant pancreatic tumors, 14% malignant endocrine tumors, 30% benign tumors,…
SUPP-004.finding: 290/1,034 (28%) developed NODM; median time to first diabetes visit 354 days (IQR 140-784). Unadjusted NODM 44% in obese vs 25% in normal/overweight. Sub-distribution HRs: obesity 2.23 (P<0.001); age 1.01/year (P=0.006); ASA 2 vs 1 2.03, ASA 3 1.61; female 0.73 (P=0.014); minimally invasive surgery 0.54 (P=0.002); benign tumor 1.43 (P=0.020). Median follow-up 45 months in survivors (Results; Table 1-2).
SUPP-004.limitations: No remnant-volume data; mixed indications; NODM date = first registry visit (lag)
SUPP-004.interpretation: National, near-complete registry: gives the base rate of diabetes after left-sided resection and the metabolic-load effect; observational for risk factors

glosses.glucose-diabetes: A Swedish national cohort of 1,034 distal pancreatectomies found new diabetes in 28%, more often with obesity.
glosses.pancreas-body-tail: Swedish national cohort of 1,034 distal pancreatectomies finding new diabetes in 28%, with obesity doubling the risk.
glosses.islets: Swedish national cohort of 1,034 distal pancreatectomies finding new diabetes in 28%, with obesity doubling the risk.
glosses.spleen: Swedish national cohort of 1,034 distal pancreatectomies finding new diabetes in 28%, with obesity doubling the risk.
glosses.distal-pancreatectomy: A Swedish national cohort of 1,034 distal pancreatectomies in which 28% developed new diabetes, with obesity doubling the risk.
glosses.total-pancreatectomy: A Swedish national cohort in which 28% developed diabetes after distal pancreatectomy, with obesity doubling the risk.
glosses.diabetes-after-surgery: A Swedish national registry cohort of 1,034 people without diabetes before distal pancreatectomy, of whom 28 percent developed it, with obesity the strongest predictor.

SUPP-005.citation: Luo L, Cao X, Qiu M, Zhu M, Yan Y, Zhang D, Zhang X. Splanchnic nerve block via transdiscal and paraspinal approach in the treatment of pain in advanced pancreatic cancer: A randomized controlled trial. Medicine (Baltimore). 2025;104(38):e44250.
SUPP-005.clinical_status: Percutaneous/EUS neurolysis is standard adjunctive practice for pancreatic cancer pain (guideline-supported); no FDA device/drug indication specific to this use; checked 2026-10-08
SUPP-005.design: Single-centre randomized trial of two percutaneous neurolytic splanchnic nerve block approaches (transdiscal vs paraspinal), fluoroscopy (DSA)-guided, 5 mL 99.5% ethanol per side; outcomes VAS, satisfaction, Karnofsky, daily morphine, complications at day 1, 3, week 1, month 1, month 3
SUPP-005.population: 34 patients with progressive pancreatic cancer pain treated in a Chinese pain department (Dec 2021-Mar 2023) with a positive diagnostic block (>=50% VAS fall)
SUPP-005.finding: Puncture time and number of fluoroscopy exposures lower in the transdiscal group (P<0.001). VAS, satisfaction and Karnofsky scores did not differ between approaches at any time point; within each group VAS at every post-procedure time point was significantly lower than baseline (P<0.001) through 3 months. No difference in total complication incidence (Results; Tables 1-3).
SUPP-005.effect: Within-group pain reduction P<0.001 at all time points; between-approach differences nil
SUPP-005.limitations: Very small; no medical-management control; single centre; 5 patients lost; morphine consumption results not clearly reported in accessed text
SUPP-005.interpretation: Randomized comparison of two techniques; the pain reduction itself is within-group (pre/post) and therefore not causally isolated from natural history or opioids

glosses.pain: A small Chinese randomized trial of two splanchnic nerve block approaches found pain scores fell from baseline through three months with either.
glosses.nerve-plexus: Small trial comparing two approaches to splanchnic nerve block, both of which lowered pain scores for three months.

SUPP-006.citation: Keum J, Lee HS, Jo JH, Chung MJ, Park JY, Park SW, Song SY, Bang S. Impact of UGT1A1 Polymorphisms on Febrile Neutropenia in Pancreatic Cancer Patients Receiving FOLFIRINOX: A Single-Center Cohort Study. Cancers (Basel). 2022;14(5):1244.
SUPP-006.clinical_status: FOLFIRINOX classified as high FN-risk regimen (NCCN); irinotecan labels (US) carry UGT1A1 dose-reduction advice for *28 homozygotes; checked 2026-10-08
SUPP-006.design: Single-centre retrospective registry cohort; Cox regression for time to febrile neutropenia (FN); predicted UGT1A1 phenotype (extensive/intermediate/poor metabolizer)
SUPP-006.population: 154 Korean patients with pancreatic cancer (7.8% resectable, 15.6% borderline, 35.7% locally advanced, 40.9% metastatic) receiving first-line FOLFIRINOX, Dec 2017-Jul 2020, with UGT1A1 genotyping
SUPP-006.finding: FN occurred in 31/154 (20.1%); median time to FN within the first four cycles. Multivariable Cox: female sex HR 2.20 (P=0.031); ECOG 1 vs 0 HR 2.83 (P=0.008); UGT1A1 intermediate metabolizer HR 4.30 (P=0.004); poor metabolizer HR 4.03 (P=0.028). Tumor in head 74.2% of FN vs 48.8% of non-FN (P=0.011). Cumulative drug doses to cycle 4 did not differ (Table 2). Background cited: grade 3/4 neutropenia 45.7-77.8% and FN 5.4-22.2% with FOLFIRINOX in prior series; NCCN v4.2021 classifies FOLFIRINOX as high FN-risk (Introduction).
SUPP-006.limitations: Single centre; retrospective; Korean population allele frequencies (UGT1A1*6 common) differ from US (*28)
SUPP-006.interpretation: Observational risk-factor analysis; supports pharmacogenetic contribution to FN risk; no intervention

glosses.fever-infection: A Korean cohort of 154 people on FOLFIRINOX found febrile neutropenia in 20%, mostly early, with higher risk in women, poorer performance status and UGT1A1 slow metabolizers.
glosses.ugt1a1-dpyd: A pancreatic cancer cohort in which UGT1A1 intermediate and poor metabolizers had about a fourfold higher febrile-neutropenia risk on FOLFIRINOX.
glosses.folfirinox: Single-center Korean cohort of 154 patients on FOLFIRINOX: 20.1% developed febrile neutropenia, mostly within four cycles, with UGT1A1 slow metabolizers at about fourfold risk.
glosses.irinotecan: A Korean cohort of 154 people on FOLFIRINOX in which febrile neutropenia affected one in five and UGT1A1 slow metabolizers had four times the hazard.
glosses.growth-factor-support: A single-center Korean cohort of 154 people on first-line FOLFIRINOX in which febrile neutropenia occurred in 20.1 percent, with female sex, poorer performance status and slow UGT1A1 metabolism as risk factors.

SUPP-007.citation: Vadhan-Raj S, McNamara MG, Venerito M, Riess H, O'Reilly EM, Overman MJ, et al. Rivaroxaban thromboprophylaxis in ambulatory patients with pancreatic cancer: Results from a pre-specified subgroup analysis of the randomized CASSINI study. Cancer Med. 2020;9(17):6196-6204.
SUPP-007.clinical_status: Rivaroxaban not FDA-labeled for ambulatory cancer VTE prophylaxis (US; Xarelto label checked DailyMed 2026-10-08); ASCO 2023 guideline permits apixaban/rivaroxaban/LMWH prophylaxis in high-risk ambulatory patients (Khorana >=2) after discussion; checked 2026-10-08
SUPP-007.design: Pre-specified subgroup of a double-blind placebo-controlled RCT; primary composite endpoint (symptomatic DVT, asymptomatic proximal DVT, any PE, VTE death) adjudicated blind; ISTH major bleeding; biomarkers
SUPP-007.population: 273 ambulatory patients with pancreatic cancer (of 841 randomized in CASSINI) starting a new systemic regimen, Khorana score >=2, no VTE on baseline screening ultrasound
SUPP-007.n: 273 (135 rivaroxaban, 138 placebo); 24/362 (6.6%) screened pancreatic patients excluded for baseline VTE
SUPP-007.finding: Up-to-day-180 ITT: primary endpoint 13/135 (9.6%) vs 18/138 (13.0%), HR 0.70 (95% CI 0.34-1.43), P=0.328. On-treatment (intervention period): 5/135 (3.7%) vs 14/138 (10.1%), HR 0.35 (0.13-0.97), P=0.034. Symptomatic events 3.7% vs 6.5%; VTE-related death 0 vs 1. Major bleeding 2 (1.5%) vs 3 (2.3%). Only 57% per arm completed the double-blind period. D-dimer fell on rivaroxaban at weeks 8 and 16 (P<0.01). Mortality not affected (HR 1.05, 0.65-1.69); ECOG >=2 HR 5.29 and Khorana >2 HR 2.47 for death (Tables 2-3; Figure 2).
SUPP-007.limitations: Subgroup (underpowered); 43% discontinued; oral drug compliance in a sick population
SUPP-007.interpretation: Randomized, placebo-controlled: supports a true antithrombotic effect while on drug; ITT null because of early discontinuation (treatment-period boundary)

glosses.blood-clots: The pancreatic subgroup of the CASSINI trial found rivaroxaban prevented clots while taken but 43% stopped it, leaving the overall result not significant.
glosses.activity-function: The pancreatic subgroup of the CASSINI trial found performance status 2 or worse carried a fivefold hazard of death.
glosses.vte-prevention: The pre-specified pancreatic subgroup of the CASSINI trial, 273 people on rivaroxaban or placebo, in which clots fell while the drug was taken but not by intention to treat because many stopped early.

SUPP-008.citation: Costamagna G, Reddy DN, Chia NH, Itoi T, Devière J, Lee KF, et al. Preoperative Biliary Drainage with Metal Stent Versus Early Surgery in Patients with Pancreatic Cancer: A Randomized Clinical Trial. Ann Surg Oncol. 2026;33(7):6801-6811.
SUPP-008.clinical_status: PBD not routinely recommended by guidelines but accepted for cholangitis, severe jaundice, delayed surgery or neoadjuvant therapy; SEMS preferred when drained (US practice); checked 2026-10-08
SUPP-008.design: Multicentre noninferiority RCT; preoperative biliary drainage (PBD) with fully covered self-expanding metal stent (SEMS) vs early surgery; primary endpoint >=1 serious adverse event (SAE) within 120 days (modified ITT); noninferiority margin 15%
SUPP-008.population: 284 patients with resectable pancreatic or periampullary cancer, serum bilirubin >=5.8 mg/dL, scheduled for primary resection at 11 centres in 9 countries
SUPP-008.finding: >=1 SAE: 40/138 (29.0%) PBD vs 36/136 (26.5%) early surgery; difference 2.5 points, one-sided upper 95% CL 11.7%, P=0.011 for noninferiority; KM 120-day SAE HR 1.1 (0.7-1.8). Protocol-specified SAEs before surgery 21/138 (15.2%) vs 7/136 (5.1%) (difference 10.1, 95% CI 2.3-17.9) but operative/postoperative SAEs 23/119 (19.3%) vs 30/130 (23.1%). SEMS placed in 140/144 (97.2%); 14/140 (10%) of early-surgery patients needed ERCP (cholangitis 4, waiting time 4, deep jaundice 3). Curative-intent surgery 119/144 vs 130/140; resection 103/118 (87.3%) vs 115/130 (88.5%). 120-day mortality 11/144 (7.6%) vs 11/140 (7.9%); pre-surgery deaths 7 vs 1, post-surgery deaths 4/119 vs 10/130; Clavien-Dindo IV-V 4/103 vs 17/115 (Table 2). Contrast with the Dutch DROP trial (plastic stents): PBD-related complications 46%, 26% cholangitis (Introduction).
SUPP-008.limitations: Open-label; SAE composite mixes stent and surgical events; survival beyond 120 days not reported in accessed text
SUPP-008.interpretation: Randomized: establishes that metal-stent PBD does not raise overall 120-day serious complications versus early surgery, reversing the generalization drawn from plastic-stent trials; shifts harm from the surgical phase to the preoperative phase

glosses.jaundice: A 2026 multinational randomized trial found that draining jaundice with a covered metal stent before a Whipple was as safe overall as operating early.
glosses.obstruction-warning: A 2026 multinational randomized trial found draining jaundice with a covered metal stent before a Whipple was as safe overall as operating early.
glosses.bile-duct-ampulla: 2026 randomized trial showing metal-stent biliary drainage before a Whipple was non-inferior to early surgery for serious complications.
glosses.whipple: A randomized trial of 284 jaundiced patients showing metal-stent drainage before a Whipple was as safe as early surgery over 120 days.
glosses.biliary-stents: A 2026 multicenter randomized trial of 284 people in which drainage with a covered metal stent before surgery was no worse than early surgery for serious complications within 120 days.

SUPP-009.citation: Boyd CA, Benarroch-Gampel J, Sheffield KM, Han Y, Kuo YF, Riall TS. The effect of depression on stage at diagnosis, treatment, and survival in pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Surgery. 2012;152(3):403-413.
SUPP-009.clinical_status: Not applicable (observational); ASCO 2024 palliative care guideline recommends routine distress screening; checked 2026-10-08
SUPP-009.design: Population-based retrospective cohort; depression defined by ICD-9 claims 3-27 months before cancer diagnosis; multivariable logistic (treatment receipt) and Cox (2-year survival) models
SUPP-009.population: 23,745 US Medicare beneficiaries with pancreatic adenocarcinoma (SEER-Medicare, 1992-2005), age >=66
SUPP-009.finding: Depression associated with older age, female sex, white race, single/widowed status and advanced stage (P<0.0001). Locoregional disease: depressed patients had lower odds of resection OR 0.63 (95% CI 0.52-0.76); 2-year survival HR 1.20 (1.09-1.32), attenuated to 1.14 (1.04-1.26) after adjusting for resection; among resected patients HR 1.34 (1.04-1.73). Distant disease: lower odds of chemotherapy OR 0.79 (0.70-0.90); after adjusting for chemotherapy HR 1.03 (0.97-1.09). Unadjusted median survival 2.1 vs 3.1 months overall; locoregional 4.1 vs 6.6 months (Results; Tables 1-4).
SUPP-009.effect: OR for resection 0.63; adjusted survival HR 1.14-1.34
SUPP-009.limitations: Claims-based depression; pre-2005 treatment era; elderly only
SUPP-009.interpretation: Observational: depression predicts less treatment and worse survival, with mediation by treatment receipt suggested by attenuation

glosses.mood-support: A US Medicare study of 23,745 patients found prior depression reduced the odds of surgery and chemotherapy, explaining much of a survival gap.
glosses.palliative-care: A US Medicare study found prior depression reduced the odds of surgery and chemotherapy, explaining much of a survival gap.

SUPP-010.citation: Pfeiffer P, Lustberg M, Näsström J, Carlsson S, Persson A, Nagahama F, et al. Calmangafodipir for Prevention of Oxaliplatin-Induced Peripheral Neuropathy: Two Placebo-Controlled, Randomized Phase 3 Studies (POLAR-A/POLAR-M). JNCI Cancer Spectr. 2022;6(6):pkac075.
SUPP-010.clinical_status: Negative phase 3; calmangafodipir not approved (US); ASCO 2020 guideline: no agents recommended for CIPN prevention; checked 2026-10-08
SUPP-010.design: Two randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials of calmangafodipir (manganese-based SOD mimetic) given before oxaliplatin; primary endpoint patient-reported moderate-to-severe CIPN (FACT/GOG-Ntx items) at 9 months; terminated early for hypersensitivity
SUPP-010.population: Patients receiving oxaliplatin-based FOLFOX for stage II-III colorectal cancer (POLAR-A, n=301) or metastatic colorectal cancer (POLAR-M, n=291)
SUPP-010.n: 592 randomized; combined primary analysis CaM 5 umol/kg n=175 vs placebo n=176
SUPP-010.finding: Moderate-to-severe CIPN at month 9: 54.3% with calmangafodipir vs 40.3% with placebo; relative risk 1.37 (95% CI 1.01-1.86), P=0.045 (Table 2) - i.e., worse. Serious hypersensitivity reactions 3.6% vs 0.8%. Trials terminated early (Results).
SUPP-010.limitations: Colorectal, not pancreatic, populations (same drug/regimen class as FOLFIRINOX oxaliplatin); early stopping
SUPP-010.interpretation: Randomized negative trial: antioxidant neuroprotection strategy failed and was associated with more neuropathy and hypersensitivity

glosses.neuropathy: Two phase 3 trials of calmangafodipir to prevent oxaliplatin neuropathy found it made neuropathy worse and caused hypersensitivity reactions.
glosses.oxaliplatin: Two randomized phase 3 trials in which the antioxidant calmangafodipir made oxaliplatin neuropathy worse and caused allergic reactions.

SUPP-011.citation: Ben-Ishay O, Dick A, Sabo E, Lahat E, Kluger Y. Rapid, intense pericholedochal fibrosis after preoperative biliary drainage: A prospective histologic study in pancreatoduodenectomy specimens. Ann Hepatobiliary Pancreat Surg. 2026;30(2):256-264.
SUPP-011.design: Prospective histologic study; Masson's trichrome digital morphometry of common bile duct wall thickness, collagen area and density; correlation with dwell time and surgical outcomes
SUPP-011.population: 46 consecutive patients undergoing pancreatoduodenectomy at a high-volume centre; 22 with preoperative plastic biliary stenting (median dwell 10 days) and 24 non-drained controls; neoadjuvant chemotherapy excluded
SUPP-011.finding: Stented ducts: wall thickness 6,554 vs 499 um (P<0.001); greater total collagen area and collagen density (both P<0.001). Fibrosis clearly evident by day 6 and not correlated with dwell time. Operative time 230 vs 230 min (P=0.98); postoperative complication rates not significantly different (Results; Tables 1-3).
SUPP-011.limitations: Small; plastic stents only; no SEMS arm; outcome data limited
SUPP-011.interpretation: Human tissue perturbation study: establishes a rapid biological response to stenting (mechanism) but shows it did not translate to worse surgical outcomes at this centre

glosses.obstruction-warning: A 2026 histology study found biliary stents cause rapid, intense fibrosis of the duct wall within days without worse surgical outcomes.
glosses.bile-duct-ampulla: Histological study showing biliary stents thicken the bile duct wall thirteen-fold within days.
glosses.biliary-stents: A prospective histology study of 46 Whipple specimens showing about thirteen-fold bile-duct wall thickening within days of a plastic stent, without a difference in surgical outcomes.

SUPP-012.citation: Seo DW, Sherman S, Dua KS, Slivka A, Roy A, Costamagna G, et al. Covered and uncovered biliary metal stents provide similar relief of biliary obstruction during neoadjuvant therapy in pancreatic cancer: a randomized trial. Gastrointest Endosc. 2019;90(4):602-612.e4.
SUPP-012.clinical_status: Both SEMS types FDA-cleared devices; practice: SEMS preferred for drainage before neoadjuvant therapy; checked 2026-10-08
SUPP-012.design: Randomized trial of fully covered vs uncovered SEMS; primary endpoint sustained biliary drainage (no reintervention) from placement to curative-intent surgery (median 110 days) or 1 year; noninferiority
SUPP-012.population: 119 patients with pancreatic cancer, jaundice/cholestasis and planned neoadjuvant therapy before pancreaticoduodenectomy (multinational; Boston Scientific sponsor)
SUPP-012.time_frame: Enrollment 2015-2018; endpoint at surgery (median 110 days) or 1 year
SUPP-012.finding: Sustained drainage 72.2% vs 72.9% (noninferiority P=0.01; registry: 39 vs 43 participants). Failure mechanisms differed: tumor ingrowth 0% vs 16.7% (registry post-hoc 0 vs 10 participants, P<0.01); migration 6.8% vs 0% (5 vs 0, P=0.03). Stent-related serious AEs 23.7% (14/59) vs 20.0% (12/60), P=0.66; acute cholecystitis with gallbladder in situ 9.3% (4/43) vs 4.8% (2/42). Completed neoadjuvant therapy without stent-related interruption: 53 vs 51 (registry). Predictors of reintervention independent of stent type: 4-cm stent length and gallbladder in situ (abstract; CT.gov results posted).
SUPP-012.effect: Sustained drainage ~72% both arms; ingrowth vs migration trade-off
SUPP-012.limitations: Abstract + registry only (full text paywalled); no plastic-stent arm
SUPP-012.interpretation: Randomized device comparison: shows that in the neoadjuvant era drainage must last months and that about 1 in 4 stents fails regardless of covering

glosses.jaundice: A randomized trial of covered versus uncovered metal stents during neoadjuvant chemotherapy found about 72% sustained drainage with either, failing by different mechanisms.
glosses.obstruction-warning: A randomized trial of covered versus uncovered metal stents during neoadjuvant chemotherapy found about 72% sustained drainage with either, failing by different mechanisms.
glosses.bile-duct-ampulla: Randomized trial showing covered and uncovered metal stents kept the bile duct open equally often (about 72%) during neoadjuvant therapy.
glosses.biliary-stents: A randomized trial of 119 people with pancreatic cancer stented before neoadjuvant therapy, in which covered and uncovered metal stents drained equally well but failed in different ways.

SUPP-013.citation: Sumiya H, Kanno Y, Koshita S, Ogawa T, Kusunose H, Sakai T, et al. Large-diameter Plastic Stents as An Option for Preoperative Biliary Drainage for Patients with Pancreatic Cancer Undergoing Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy. Korean J Gastroenterol. 2026;86(3):227-235.
SUPP-013.clinical_status: Both stent types in routine US use; checked 2026-10-08
SUPP-013.design: Retrospective single-centre comparison of plastic stents (PS, n=33; 27 were >=10 Fr) vs fully covered SEMS (n=14); recurrent biliary obstruction (RBO) and non-RBO adverse events
SUPP-013.population: 47 consecutive Japanese patients with pancreatic cancer drained before neoadjuvant chemotherapy (Jun 2012-Sep 2024) and followed to the resection decision
SUPP-013.finding: RBO 39% (PS) vs 7.1% (FCSEMS), P=0.081; time to RBO 126 days vs not reached (P=0.046). Non-RBO AEs (pancreatitis, cholecystitis) 15% vs 43% (P=0.061). Overall AEs 45% vs 43% (P=1.0). Subgroup PS >=10 Fr vs FCSEMS: no significant differences (Results; Tables 1-6).
SUPP-013.interpretation: Observational bridge from trial setting to real-world neoadjuvant practice: trade-off between occlusion (plastic) and pancreatitis/cholecystitis (metal)

glosses.obstruction-warning: A Japanese series of 47 people drained before neoadjuvant chemotherapy found plastic stents re-blocked far more often than covered metal stents.
glosses.bile-duct-ampulla: Retrospective comparison of plastic and metal stents for pre-operative biliary drainage.
glosses.biliary-stents: A retrospective Japanese comparison of 47 people drained before neoadjuvant chemotherapy, in which plastic stents blocked more often and metal stents caused more pancreatitis and cholecystitis.

SUPP-014.citation: Groarke JD, Crawford J, Collins SM, Lubaczewski S, Roeland EJ, Naito T, et al. Ponsegromab for the Treatment of Cancer Cachexia. N Engl J Med. 2024;391(24):2291-2303.
SUPP-014.clinical_status: Investigational (not FDA-approved); phase 3 in pancreatic cancer cachexia recruiting (NCT06989437, start 2025-10, n~982); checked 2026-10-08
SUPP-014.design: Phase 2 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, 4-arm (placebo, 100, 200, 400 mg SC every 4 weeks x3); primary endpoint change in body weight at 12 weeks (Bayesian); secondary appetite/cachexia symptoms (FAACT), digital physical activity, safety
SUPP-014.population: 187 patients with cancer cachexia and serum GDF-15 >=1,500 pg/mL: 40% non-small-cell lung, 32% pancreatic, 29% colorectal cancer (PROACC-1; international)
SUPP-014.finding: Weight change vs placebo at 12 weeks: +1.22 kg (95% credible interval 0.37-2.25) at 100 mg, +1.92 (0.92-2.97) at 200 mg, +2.81 (1.55-4.08) at 400 mg (abstract; registry posterior-median differences 1.33, 2.08, 3.00 kg). FAACT anorexia-cachexia subscale LS-mean difference vs placebo +4.24 (100 mg, P=0.011) and +4.11 (400 mg, P=0.014); 5-item anorexia scale +2.35 and +2.30 (P~0.01). Total activity (vector magnitude) +2,203 (84-4,322) at 400 mg (P=0.044); non-sedentary activity fell -37.7 min on placebo vs +12.1 at 400 mg. Adverse events 70% ponsegromab vs 80% placebo (abstract; CT.gov results posted).
SUPP-014.effect: Dose-dependent weight gain up to ~2.8 kg over 12 weeks
SUPP-014.limitations: Phase 2; pancreatic subgroup results not in accessed text; survival not an endpoint
SUPP-014.interpretation: Randomized placebo-controlled perturbation of a single cytokine in humans: GDF-15 blockade reverses weight loss and improves appetite -> GDF-15 is a causal driver of cachexia in a biomarker-selected population including pancreatic cancer

glosses.weight-loss-cachexia: A phase 2 randomized trial of the GDF-15 antibody ponsegromab in 187 people with cancer cachexia (32% pancreatic) found dose-dependent weight gain up to 2.8 kg at 12 weeks.
glosses.fatigue: A phase 2 trial of the GDF-15 antibody ponsegromab found weight gain and more daily activity than placebo at 12 weeks in cancer cachexia.
glosses.nutrition: A phase 2 trial of the GDF-15 antibody ponsegromab found dose-dependent weight gain in cancer cachexia at 12 weeks.
glosses.activity-function: A phase 2 trial of the GDF-15 antibody ponsegromab found weight gain and more activity in cancer cachexia at 12 weeks.
glosses.palliative-care: A phase 2 trial of the GDF-15 antibody ponsegromab showed that cancer-related appetite loss has a treatable cytokine basis.
glosses.cachexia-treatments: The phase 2 PROACC-1 trial of ponsegromab in 187 people with cancer cachexia and high GDF-15, a third with pancreatic cancer, showing dose-dependent weight gain of up to 2.8 kg over 12 weeks.
glosses.cachexia-research: The randomized placebo-controlled phase 2 of the anti-GDF-15 antibody ponsegromab in 187 patients with cancer cachexia, a third with pancreatic cancer, showing dose-dependent weight gain up to 2.81 kg over twelve weeks.

SUPP-015.citation: Wochner R, Clauss D, Nattenmüller J, Tjaden C, Bruckner T, Kauczor HU, et al. Impact of progressive resistance training on CT quantified muscle and adipose tissue compartments in pancreatic cancer patients. PLoS One. 2020;15(11):e0242785.
SUPP-015.clinical_status: Exercise recommended during and after treatment (ASCO/ACS guidance); checked 2026-10-08
SUPP-015.design: Secondary analysis of an RCT; routine CT at L3/4 quantified muscle area, muscle density, SMI, fat compartments and visceral-to-subcutaneous fat ratio (VFR) before/after intervention; overall survival analysis
SUPP-015.population: Pancreatic cancer patients (mostly resected, Heidelberg) enrolled in the SUPPORT randomized trial of 6-month progressive resistance training (supervised or home-based) vs usual care
SUPP-015.n: 65 randomized; 53 with baseline CT; 28 with paired CT
SUPP-015.finding: No significant effect of resistance training on any CT body-composition compartment (all P>0.05; effect sizes omega2p <0.02). Muscle area correlated with muscle strength (r=0.57-0.85; P<0.001). High baseline VFR (>=1.3) predicted poor OS: median 14.6 vs 45.3 months (P=0.012). Loss vs gain of SMI: median OS 24.6 vs 50.8 months (P=0.049). Parent trial (Wiskemann 2019, abstract): strength improved in some muscle groups with supervised training; adherence 64-78%; no body-weight difference (Results; Tables 1-6).
SUPP-015.effect: Training effect on body composition: null; SMI loss OS 24.6 vs 50.8 months
SUPP-015.interpretation: Randomized intervention replicating the prognostic muscle-loss association in resected patients while challenging whether training alone alters muscle mass

glosses.weight-loss-cachexia: A CT analysis of a German randomized trial found six months of resistance training did not change muscle area, while muscle loss predicted shorter survival.
glosses.nutrition: A CT analysis of a German randomized trial found six months of resistance training did not change muscle area.
glosses.activity-function: A CT analysis of that trial found six months of resistance training did not change muscle area, while muscle loss predicted shorter survival.
glosses.cachexia-treatments: A secondary analysis of a randomized trial of six months of resistance training in 65 people with pancreatic cancer, finding no change in CT-measured muscle.
glosses.cachexia-research: A randomized trial of six months of progressive resistance training in 65 pancreatic cancer patients, which changed no CT-measured body compartment while confirming that muscle loss tracks survival.

SUPP-016.citation: Lee NR, Hwang HK, Lee H, Kang CM. Oral Protein Supplements Might Improve Nutritional Status and Quality of Life in Elderly Patients after Standard Pancreatic Resection. Nutrients. 2024;16(17):2988.
SUPP-016.clinical_status: Oral nutrition supplements are standard supportive care (ESPEN/ASCO guidance); checked 2026-10-08
SUPP-016.design: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of a daily 18 g protein supplement for 6 weeks vs isocaloric carbohydrate placebo; outcomes dietary intake, bioimpedance (muscle mass, phase angle), walking speed, QoL (linear mixed models)
SUPP-016.population: Elderly Korean patients after pylorus-preserving pancreatoduodenectomy or distal pancreatectomy (single centre)
SUPP-016.finding: Protein intake 77.3+/-5.3 g vs 56.7+/-6.0 g (P=0.049); supplement group had better QoL, nutritional status and faster walking speed than placebo (group x time interactions reported in Tables 2-4); protein intake correlated positively with muscle mass and phase angle (Results).
SUPP-016.effect: Protein intake +~20 g/day; functional/QoL gains reported
SUPP-016.limitations: Single centre; exact effect sizes for walking speed/QoL not extracted; short follow-up
SUPP-016.interpretation: Randomized, blinded nutritional perturbation after resection: supports that the nutritional arm of weight/muscle loss is partly modifiable

glosses.fatigue: A blinded Korean trial found extra protein after pancreatic surgery improved walking speed and quality of life in elderly patients.
glosses.nutrition: A blinded Korean trial found an extra 18 g of protein a day after pancreatic surgery raised intake and improved walking speed and quality of life in elderly patients.
glosses.life-after-whipple: A blinded Korean trial found extra protein after pancreatic surgery improved walking speed and quality of life in elderly patients.
glosses.cachexia-treatments: A double-blind trial of 41 older people after pancreatic resection in which 18 g of daily protein supplement for six weeks improved intake, walking speed and quality of life.
glosses.cachexia-research: A blinded randomized trial of 18 grams of daily protein supplement after pancreatic resection, which raised protein intake and improved walking speed and quality of life.

SUPP-017.citation: Ngo-Huang A, Parker NH, Bruera E, Lee RE, Simpson R, O'Connor DP, et al. Home-Based Exercise Prehabilitation During Preoperative Treatment for Pancreatic Cancer Is Associated With Improvement in Physical Function and Quality of Life. Integr Cancer Ther. 2019;18:1534735419894061.
SUPP-017.clinical_status: Prehabilitation offered at many US centres; not a regulated product; checked 2026-10-08
SUPP-017.design: Prospective single-arm trial of home-based prehabilitation (>=60 min/week each of moderate aerobic and strengthening exercise) with accelerometry; physical function (6MWT, 5xSTS, grip, gait speed, PROMIS) and FACT-Hep at baseline and preoperative restaging
SUPP-017.population: 50 patients with potentially resectable pancreatic adenocarcinoma receiving preoperative chemotherapy and/or chemoradiation at MD Anderson (mean age 66)
SUPP-017.finding: 6MWT 462.5+/-82.7 m to 488.2+/-93.1 m (P=0.001; clinically meaningful); 5xSTS 11.4 to 10.6 s (P=0.049); gait speed improved (P=0.009). Increases in self-reported aerobic exercise, MVPA and light activity were associated with 6MWT gains (beta 0.19, 0.18, 0.08) and self-reported physical function; more light activity associated with higher HRQOL (beta 0.03, P=0.02) and more sedentary time with lower HRQOL (beta -0.02, P=0.01) (Table 2).
SUPP-017.interpretation: Single-arm: feasibility and dose-response association, not causal proof of benefit

glosses.fatigue: A home-exercise study during preoperative treatment found improved walking distance and linked sedentary time to lower quality of life.
glosses.activity-function: A US single-arm study of home exercise during preoperative treatment found improved walking distance, sit-to-stand time and gait speed in 50 patients.
glosses.cachexia-research: A single-arm trial of home-based exercise during preoperative treatment in 50 patients, which improved six-minute walk distance by 25.7 meters.

SUPP-018.citation: Florez Bedoya CA, Cardoso ACF, Parker N, Ngo-Huang A, Petzel MQ, Kim MP, et al. Exercise during preoperative therapy increases tumor vascularity in pancreatic tumor patients. Sci Rep. 2019;9(1):13966.
SUPP-018.clinical_status: Preclinical/translational; exercise is standard supportive advice; checked 2026-10-08
SUPP-018.design: Preclinical perturbation (exercise + gemcitabine in PDX) plus human tissue comparison; CD31 immunofluorescence vessel counts, microvessel density, vessel morphology; tumor regression/regrowth in mice
SUPP-018.population: Patient-derived xenograft (PDX) PDAC mice treated with gemcitabine with/without treadmill exercise; and resected human PDAC specimens from 23 prehabilitation-trial participants vs 15 matched historical controls
SUPP-018.n: Mice: groups per experiment (numbers in figure legends); humans: 23 prehab vs 15 controls
SUPP-018.time_frame: Mouse experiments and human specimens from 2016-2018 trial
SUPP-018.finding: Mice: exercise remodeled tumor vasculature, accelerated regression and delayed regrowth with gemcitabine; vessels per 200x field 24.0 vs 4.6 (P=0.001); no change in hENT1 expression. Humans: prehab tumors had twice the vessels per field (7.0+/-5.07 vs 3.53+/-2.44, P=0.01), higher microvessel density (17.97+/-9.96 vs 11.27+/-5.51 CD31+ units/field, P=0.02), more elongated vessels (P=0.03) and open lumens; no difference in fibrosis or inflammation grade (Figure 4).
SUPP-018.effect: ~2-fold vessel density in exercised patients' tumors
SUPP-018.limitations: Small human sample; chemotherapy efficacy in humans not tested
SUPP-018.interpretation: Causal in mice (perturbation); associational in humans (historical controls); links a daily-life behavior to tumor stromal vasculature

glosses.activity-function: A US study found tumors from patients who exercised before surgery had twice the vessel density, with mouse experiments showing better gemcitabine response.
glosses.cachexia-research: A study of mouse tumors and resected human specimens finding roughly twice the vessel density in tumors from patients who exercised during preoperative therapy.

SUPP-019.citation: Kurz E, Hirsch CA, Dalton T, Shadaloey SA, Khodadadi-Jamayran A, Miller G, et al. Exercise-induced engagement of the IL-15/IL-15Ralpha axis promotes anti-tumor immunity in pancreatic cancer. Cancer Cell. 2022;40(7):720-737.e5.
SUPP-019.design: Preclinical perturbation with single-cell RNA sequencing of tumor immune infiltrates, depletion/blockade experiments; human immunohistochemistry (CD8, granzyme B) and survival association
SUPP-019.population: Orthotopic/KPC-derived mouse PDAC models with treadmill aerobic exercise; IL-15 super-agonist (NIZ985) and anti-PD-1 experiments; human PDAC resection specimens from patients in a prospective preoperative exercise trial vs matched historical controls
SUPP-019.n: Mouse cohorts per experiment; human exercise cohort vs historical controls (numbers in figure legends)
SUPP-019.finding: Exercise reduced PDAC growth in mice via CD8 T cells; promoted mobilization and tumor accumulation of IL-15Ralpha+ CD8 T cells (required for protection); reduced myeloid-derived suppressor cells. NIZ985 attenuated growth, prolonged survival and enhanced chemotherapy sensitivity; exercise or NIZ985 sensitized tumors to anti-PD-1. In patients, preoperative exercise was associated with significantly more intratumoral CD8 T cells and a trend to higher granzyme B vs historical controls, and higher median survival among exercise-cohort patients with high CD8/GZMB (Results; figures).
SUPP-019.effect: Qualitative (significant CD8 increase; survival in mice prolonged)
SUPP-019.limitations: Mouse-to-human transfer; historical controls; immunotherapy benefit in PDAC remains unproven clinically (cross-reference TX/TME)
SUPP-019.interpretation: Perturbation/rescue in mice establishes an exercise -> IL-15 -> CD8 axis; human data associational

glosses.activity-function: A US study found exercise recruited CD8 T cells into mouse tumors through IL-15 signaling and more CD8 T cells in tumors of exercising patients.
glosses.cachexia-research: A mouse and human study establishing an exercise-to-interleukin-15-to-CD8 pathway, with more CD8 T cells in tumors from patients who exercised before surgery.

SUPP-020.citation: Domínguez-Muñoz JE, Nieto-Garcia L, López-Díaz J, Lariño-Noia J, Abdulkader I, Iglesias-Garcia J. Impact of the treatment of pancreatic exocrine insufficiency on survival of patients with unresectable pancreatic cancer: a retrospective analysis. BMC Cancer. 2018;18(1):534.
SUPP-020.clinical_status: PERT guideline-recommended for symptomatic exocrine insufficiency in pancreatic cancer (UEG 2025; NCCN supportive care); survival benefit unproven; checked 2026-10-08
SUPP-020.design: Retrospective two-group comparison: standard oncologic care (Group 1, n=86) vs care in a unit that evaluated exocrine insufficiency and gave PERT when indicated (Group 2, n=74); Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression
SUPP-020.population: 160 patients with unresectable, pathologically confirmed pancreatic cancer (78.7% stage IV; mean age 70.5) at a Spanish centre
SUPP-020.time_frame: Single centre; overall mortality 86.9% by study end
SUPP-020.finding: Median survival Group 2 189 days (95% CI 167-211) vs Group 1 95 days (75-115); HR 2.12 (1.49-3.00), P<0.001. Chemotherapy use differed: 71.6% vs 46.5% (P<0.001). Multivariable (age, stage): chemotherapy HR 3.69 (2.33-5.85) and PERT HR 1.81 (1.23-2.66; P=0.002) independently associated with longer survival. In patients with >10% weight loss, PERT HR 2.52 (1.55-4.11) (Table 2, Figures 1-2).
SUPP-020.effect: Adjusted HR 1.81 for survival with PERT (observational)
SUPP-020.limitations: Retrospective; non-randomized group assignment; PERT given to 66% of Group 2 only
SUPP-020.interpretation: Observational association with strong confounding-by-indication and by chemotherapy eligibility; hypothesis-generating only

glosses.digestion-enzymes: A Spanish cohort of 160 unresectable patients found enzyme use associated with longer survival, but enzyme users also received chemotherapy far more often.
glosses.enzyme-replacement: A retrospective Spanish comparison of 160 people with unresectable pancreatic cancer in which enzyme replacement was associated with longer survival but treated patients also received more chemotherapy.

SUPP-021.citation: Landers A, Brown H, Strother M. The effectiveness of pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy for malabsorption in advanced pancreatic cancer, a pilot study. Palliat Care. 2019;12:1178224218825270.
SUPP-021.clinical_status: PERT FDA-approved for exocrine insufficiency; checked 2026-10-08
SUPP-021.design: Prospective single-arm pilot; pancrelipase 25,000 IU (Creon) started with meals; malabsorption symptom checklist, EORTC QLQ-C30 and QLQ-PAN26 at baseline, 1 and 3 weeks
SUPP-021.population: 44 patients with metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma referred to a specialist palliative care service (New Zealand); 29 completed
SUPP-021.n: 44 enrolled; 29 completed (completers had better ECOG and higher weight)
SUPP-021.finding: Within 1 week: diarrhoea score 26 to 8 (P<0.005); pancreatic pain 47 to 33 and hepatic pain 24 to 11 (P<0.05). At 3 weeks: pancreatic pain 47 to 26 and bloating/gas 46 to 26 (P<0.005) (Tables 1-2).
SUPP-021.effect: Symptom score reductions of ~18-20 points on EORTC scales
SUPP-021.interpretation: Uncontrolled: symptom improvement plausible but confounded by concurrent care and dropout of the sickest

glosses.pain: A pilot study in 29 people with metastatic disease found enzyme replacement reduced pain, diarrhea and bloating scores within one to three weeks.
glosses.digestion-enzymes: A pilot study in 29 people with metastatic pancreatic cancer found enzyme replacement reduced diarrhea within a week and pain and bloating within three weeks.
glosses.fatigue: A pilot study found enzyme replacement relieved diarrhea and bloating within weeks in metastatic pancreatic cancer.
glosses.nausea-bowel: A pilot study in 29 people with metastatic disease found enzyme replacement reduced diarrhea within one week and bloating within three.
glosses.palliative-care: A pilot study found enzyme replacement relieved diarrhea, pain and bloating within weeks in metastatic pancreatic cancer.
glosses.enzyme-replacement: A single-arm pilot in 44 people with metastatic pancreatic cancer in which enzyme capsules reduced diarrhea within a week and pain and bloating within three.

SUPP-022.citation: Hamauchi S, Furuse J, Takano T, Munemoto Y, Furuya K, Baba H, et al. A multicenter, open-label, single-arm study of anamorelin (ONO-7643) in advanced gastrointestinal cancer patients with cancer cachexia. Cancer. 2019;125(23):4294-4302.
SUPP-022.clinical_status: Anamorelin approved in Japan (2021) for cachexia in GI/lung cancers; not FDA-approved (US); checked 2026-10-08
SUPP-022.design: Phase 2 open-label single-arm; anamorelin 100 mg daily x 12 weeks; primary endpoint proportion maintaining or gaining lean body mass (DEXA) at all time points
SUPP-022.population: 50 Japanese patients with unresectable colorectal (n=40), gastric (n=5) or pancreatic (n=5) cancer and cachexia (>=5% weight loss/6 months, anorexia, plus biochemical/functional criteria); 19 centres, Feb 2017-Apr 2018
SUPP-022.finding: LBM responders 63.3% (95% CI 48.3-76.6); LS-mean change LBM +1.89+/-0.36 kg and body weight +1.41+/-0.61 kg; appetite items improved. AEs 79.6%; treatment-related: GGT increase 8.2%, diabetes mellitus 6.1%, hyperglycemia 6.1%, prolonged QRS 6.1% (Results; Tables 1-2).
SUPP-022.limitations: Only 5 pancreatic patients; open-label; Japanese population
SUPP-022.interpretation: Uncontrolled: shows a plausible anabolic/orexigenic effect but no causal isolation

glosses.weight-loss-cachexia: A Japanese single-arm study of anamorelin in 50 people with gastrointestinal cancer cachexia (5 pancreatic) found lean mass gain and hyperglycemia in 6%.
glosses.cachexia-treatments: A single-arm Japanese phase 2 study of anamorelin in 50 people with gastrointestinal cancer cachexia, five with pancreatic cancer, showing lean-mass gain with raised blood sugar in some.
glosses.cachexia-research: A single-arm phase 2 of the ghrelin-receptor agonist anamorelin in 50 patients with gastrointestinal cancer cachexia, raising lean body mass by 1.89 kg with raised blood sugar in about 6 percent.

SUPP-023.citation: Nishimura A, Hamauchi S, Notsu A, Fushiki K, Oshima K, Tsushima T, et al. Real-world data of anamorelin in advanced gastrointestinal cancer patients with cancer cachexia. BMC Palliat Care. 2024;23(1):214.
SUPP-023.clinical_status: Approved in Japan; not FDA-approved; checked 2026-10-08
SUPP-023.design: Retrospective single-centre cohort; response defined as weight maintenance/gain plus improved appetite at every 3-week evaluation; discontinuation reasons; association with chemotherapy disease control
SUPP-023.population: 74 patients with unresectable/advanced colorectal (27), gastric (20) or pancreatic (27, 36.5%) cancer and cachexia treated with anamorelin at Shizuoka Cancer Center, Apr 2017-Aug 2022; ECOG >=2 in 27%
SUPP-023.n: 74 (44 evaluable for response after excluding early discontinuation)
SUPP-023.finding: 28/74 (38%) discontinued within 3 weeks (grade 1-2 AEs 15, ileus 3, grade 3 fatigue 1, PD 1, censored 6, unknown 3). Responders 63.6% (95% CI 47.8-77.6) of evaluable; age >=75 attenuated response (P=0.03). Responders had higher disease control on chemotherapy: 21/28 (75.0%) vs 6/16 (37.5%), OR 4.80 (1.11-23.2), P=0.024 (Table 3).
SUPP-023.limitations: Retrospective; pancreatic subgroup outcomes not separately reported in accessed text
SUPP-023.interpretation: Observational: real-world tolerability boundary (ileus/early stopping) and a confounded link between response and tumor control

glosses.weight-loss-cachexia: A Japanese real-world study of anamorelin found 38% stopped within three weeks and that responders had higher chemotherapy disease control.
glosses.cachexia-treatments: A retrospective Japanese cohort of 74 people on anamorelin in which 38 percent stopped within three weeks and responders had higher disease control on chemotherapy.
glosses.cachexia-research: A 74-patient real-world cohort of anamorelin, 27 with pancreatic cancer, documenting 38 percent discontinuation within three weeks and a confounded link between cachexia response and chemotherapy disease control.

SUPP-024.citation: Frere C, Gourgou S, Winter A, Gauthier L, Canivet C, Crichi B, et al. Risk Assessment Models for Predicting Venous Thromboembolism in Patients with Pancreatic Cancer. Cancers (Basel). 2025;17(4):597.
SUPP-024.clinical_status: Khorana score embedded in ASCO 2023 guidance for prophylaxis decisions; checked 2026-10-08
SUPP-024.design: Prospective cohort; competing-risk cumulative incidence of VTE (PE, DVT, visceral vein thrombosis, catheter thrombosis; symptomatic or incidental); head-to-head time-dependent c-index of Khorana, PROTECHT and ONKOTEV scores
SUPP-024.population: 762 newly diagnosed pancreatic cancer patients receiving ambulatory chemotherapy in the French multicentre prospective BACAP cohort (37.6% metastatic; 61% platinum-based, 33.9% gemcitabine-based)
SUPP-024.finding: 6-month VTE 73/762 (9.6% crude; cumulative incidence 16.4%, 95% CI 13.8-19.1 in competing-risk analysis): PE 17 (23.3%), DVT 17 (23.3%), visceral vein thrombosis 29 (31.5%), catheter 4, combined 6; incidental 41 (56.2%), symptomatic 32 (43.8%). Over median 40 months, 195 (25.6%) developed VTE and 354 (46.5%) died. C-index: Khorana 0.50 (0.46-0.55), PROTECHT 0.50, ONKOTEV 0.53 (0.48-0.58); 99.0% classified high-risk by Khorana (Tables 2-3). Parent BACAP paper (Frere 2020, abstract): 731 patients, VTE 20.8% at median 19.3 months, cumulative 8.07% at 3 and 19.21% at 12 months; VTE associated with shorter OS (HR 2.02, 1.57-2.60).
SUPP-024.limitations: French cohort; prophylaxis use not detailed in accessed text; visceral vein thrombosis included (often excluded in trials)
SUPP-024.interpretation: Prospective incidence estimate and a decisive negative test of risk-score discrimination within pancreatic cancer

glosses.blood-clots: A French prospective cohort of 762 people found a 16.4% six-month clot incidence and showed that standard risk scores cannot discriminate within pancreatic cancer.
glosses.spleen: French cohort of 762 patients showing 16% cumulative venous thromboembolism at six months, a third of events in abdominal veins.
glosses.smv-portal-vein: French cohort of 762 patients showing 16% cumulative venous thromboembolism at six months, a third of events in abdominal veins.
glosses.splenic-vessels: French cohort of 762 patients showing 16% cumulative venous thromboembolism at six months, a third of events in abdominal veins.
glosses.vte-prevention: A French prospective cohort of 762 people with pancreatic cancer starting chemotherapy, with a 16.4 percent six-month clot incidence and risk scores that could not rank who would clot.

SUPP-025.citation: Ullah F, Song J, Rojas Hernandez CM, Kroll MH, Escalante CP, Toale KM. Safety and Effectiveness of Direct Oral Anticoagulants for the Treatment of Gastrointestinal Cancer-Associated Venous Thromboembolism. Oncologist. 2023;28(11):e1005-e1016.
SUPP-025.clinical_status: Apixaban and rivaroxaban FDA-approved for VTE treatment (labels checked DailyMed 2026-10-08); ASCO 2023 guideline: DOACs or LMWH for cancer VTE, with caution for GI/GU luminal lesions; checked 2026-10-08
SUPP-025.design: Retrospective chart-review cohort; primary outcomes major bleeding (MB), clinically relevant non-major bleeding (CRNMB), recurrent VTE; cumulative incidence comparisons
SUPP-025.population: 433 patients with gastrointestinal cancers and VTE treated with apixaban (n=300) or rivaroxaban (n=133) for >=6 months at MD Anderson
SUPP-025.finding: MB 3.7% (95% CI 2.1-5.9); CRNMB 5.3% (3.4-7.9); recurrent VTE 7.4% (5.1-10.3) over >=6 months; cumulative incidences of CRNMB and recurrence not significantly different between DOACs (Results; Tables 1-5).
SUPP-025.limitations: No LMWH comparator; retrospective; pancreatic subgroup not extracted
SUPP-025.interpretation: Observational treatment cohort in the GI-cancer population where trial-level DOAC GI bleeding signals (Hokusai-VTE Cancer edoxaban; SELECT-D rivaroxaban) were raised; apixaban (Caravaggio) did not show excess

glosses.blood-clots: A US cohort of 433 people with gastrointestinal cancers on apixaban or rivaroxaban found major bleeding in 3.7% and recurrent clots in 7.4%.
glosses.vte-prevention: A retrospective cohort of 433 people with gastrointestinal cancers treated with apixaban or rivaroxaban for clots, with 3.7 percent major bleeding and 7.4 percent recurrence and no difference between drugs.

SUPP-026.citation: Smith EM, Pang H, Cirrincione C, Fleishman S, Paskett ED, Ahles T, et al. Effect of duloxetine on pain, function, and quality of life among patients with chemotherapy-induced painful peripheral neuropathy: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2013;309(13):1359-1367.
SUPP-026.clinical_status: Duloxetine FDA-approved for several pain indications but not specifically CIPN; ASCO 2020 CIPN guideline recommends duloxetine for established painful CIPN (moderate recommendation); checked 2026-10-08
SUPP-026.design: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover (CALGB 170601); duloxetine 30 mg x1 week then 60 mg x4 weeks; primary endpoint BPI-SF average pain change during initial 5-week period; stratified by drug class (taxane vs platinum)
SUPP-026.population: 231 patients with >=grade 1 sensory CIPN and average pain >=4/10 after paclitaxel or oxaliplatin (later docetaxel, nab-paclitaxel, cisplatin allowed), 8 NCI cooperative networks, 2008-2011
SUPP-026.finding: Initial period mean decrease in average pain: duloxetine 1.06 (95% CI 0.72-1.40) vs placebo 0.34 (0.01-0.66), P=0.003; difference 0.73 (0.26-1.20); effect size 0.513. Any pain decrease 59% vs 38% (Results; Figure 2). Stratification by platinum vs taxane; the published secondary analysis (Smith 2017) reported oxaliplatin-treated patients as more likely to respond (lead, not re-extracted).
SUPP-026.limitations: Mixed tumor types; short; oxaliplatin-specific numbers not in accessed main text
SUPP-026.interpretation: Randomized, blinded: duloxetine reduces established painful CIPN (symptomatic treatment, not prevention)

glosses.neuropathy: A US randomized crossover trial of duloxetine for painful chemotherapy neuropathy found a 0.73-point greater fall in pain than placebo.
glosses.oxaliplatin: A blinded crossover trial in 231 people with painful chemotherapy neuropathy in which duloxetine modestly reduced pain versus placebo.

SUPP-027.citation: Navari RM, Qin R, Ruddy KJ, Liu H, Powell SF, Bajaj M, et al. Olanzapine for the Prevention of Chemotherapy-Induced Nausea and Vomiting. N Engl J Med. 2016;375(2):134-142.
SUPP-027.clinical_status: Olanzapine off-label for CINV (US); ASCO 2020 antiemetic guideline includes olanzapine for HEC and as option for MEC; checked 2026-10-08
SUPP-027.design: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3; olanzapine 10 mg days 1-4 added to dexamethasone, NK1 antagonist and 5-HT3 antagonist; primary endpoint no nausea
SUPP-027.population: 380 chemotherapy-naive patients receiving highly emetogenic chemotherapy (cisplatin >=70 mg/m2 or cyclophosphamide-doxorubicin), US Alliance network
SUPP-027.finding: No nausea: 0-24 h 74% vs 45% (P=0.002); 25-120 h 42% vs 25% (P=0.002); overall 37% vs 22% (P=0.002). Complete response 86% vs 65%, 67% vs 52%, 64% vs 41% (P<0.001, 0.007, <0.001). Severe sedation day 2 in 5% of olanzapine patients; no grade 5 events (Results; Tables 1-3).
SUPP-027.limitations: Boundary: pancreatic regimens (FOLFIRINOX, gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel) are classified moderately emetogenic, so extrapolation is by regimen class
SUPP-027.interpretation: Randomized, blinded: olanzapine adds nausea control to triple prophylaxis for highly emetogenic regimens

glosses.nausea-bowel: A US randomized trial found adding olanzapine to standard prevention raised the no-nausea rate from 22% to 37% with highly emetogenic chemotherapy.

SUPP-028.citation: Kristjanson M, Lambert P, Decker KM, Bruin S, Tingey E, Skrabek P. Steroid-Induced Hyperglycemia and Its Effect on Outcomes of R-CHOP Chemotherapy for Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma. Curr Oncol. 2023;30(12):10142-10151.
SUPP-028.clinical_status: Not applicable; ADA/ASCO supportive-care guidance for steroid hyperglycemia monitoring; checked 2026-10-08
SUPP-028.design: Retrospective registry-linked chart review; steroid-induced hyperglycemia vs euglycemia; infection/febrile neutropenia and overall survival
SUPP-028.population: 188 patients with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma treated with R-CHOP (prednisone 100 mg x5 days per cycle) in Manitoba, 2010-2014
SUPP-028.finding: Patients destined to become hyperglycemic did so during the first cycle; 12.2% had early and sustained hyperglycemia; no significant differences in OS or infection rates between hyperglycemic and euglycemic groups (Results; Discussion). Cited prior work: 37% of hyper-CVAD patients with >=2 glucose >=200 mg/dL and shorter survival (29 vs 88 months).
SUPP-028.effect: 12.2% early sustained hyperglycemia; outcome difference null
SUPP-028.limitations: Non-pancreatic population and a different steroid schedule than antiemetic dexamethasone; transfer to pancreatic regimens is an assumption; no pancreatic-specific study located (searches recorded in shortfalls)
SUPP-028.interpretation: Observational; shows timing (first cycle) and a null outcome association in lymphoma

glosses.glucose-diabetes: A lymphoma cohort found steroid-induced hyperglycemia appeared in the first chemotherapy cycle in 12% (not a pancreatic population).
glosses.nausea-bowel: A lymphoma cohort found steroid-induced hyperglycemia appeared in the first chemotherapy cycle in 12% (not a pancreatic population).
glosses.diabetes-after-surgery: A Canadian lymphoma cohort on high-dose prednisone in which steroid-induced hyperglycemia appeared in the first cycle in those who developed it, recorded here as a boundary study outside pancreatic cancer.

SUPP-029.citation: Johns Hopkins University (Khashab MA, sponsor-investigator). EUS-guided Gastroenterostomy Versus Enteral Stenting for Palliation of Malignant Gastric Outlet Obstruction: A Randomized Clinical Trial. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03259763; results first posted 2026-07-06 (no peer-reviewed publication located as of 2026-10-08).
