SUPP-029.clinical_status: Lumen-apposing metal stents FDA-cleared; EUS-GE for GOO is off-label device use in the US; practice: offered at expert centres; checked 2026-10-08
SUPP-029.design: Multicentre randomized trial; EUS-guided gastroenterostomy with lumen-apposing metal stent vs enteral (duodenal) self-expanding metal stent; primary endpoint recurrence of gastric outlet obstruction at 12 months; secondary technical/clinical success, adverse events, length of stay, reintervention,…
SUPP-029.population: 112 patients with malignant gastric outlet obstruction at Yale, Johns Hopkins, Wake Forest, McGill, IECED (Ecuador) and Hopital Prive des Peupliers (France); enrollment Oct 2020-Jun 2025
SUPP-029.finding: Registry-posted results: GOO recurrence at 12 months 0% (95% CI 0-0) EUS-GE vs 15.4% (5.3-25.4) ES; reintervention 0% vs 15.4%; clinical success at 1 week 50 vs 42 participants; procedure length 24.3+/-12.5 vs 15.8+/-8.1 min; adverse events 4 vs 4 at 12 months; post-procedure stay 0.7+/-0.6 vs 0.9+/-1.5 days; SF-36 at 3 months similar across domains (e.g., physical functioning 38.7 vs 44.1) (CT.gov outcome measures).
SUPP-029.limitations: Registry-only source; no peer-reviewed methods/limitations; denominators partly implicit
SUPP-029.interpretation: Randomized: supports lower recurrence/reintervention with EUS-GE than duodenal stenting; consistent with DRA-GOO (Teoh 2024/2025, retracted and republished; abstract-only lead: reintervention 4% vs 29%, RR 0.15)

glosses.obstruction-warning: A multicenter randomized trial (registry results) found no recurrence of gastric outlet obstruction at 12 months after endoscopic gastroenterostomy versus 15.4% after a duodenal stent.
glosses.duodenum: Johns Hopkins randomized trial showing endoscopic gastroenterostomy had no recurrent obstruction at 12 months versus 15% with duodenal stents.
glosses.stomach: Johns Hopkins randomized trial showing endoscopic gastroenterostomy had no recurrent obstruction at 12 months versus 15% with duodenal stents.

SUPP-030.citation: Kim CA, Lelond S, Daeninck PJ, Rabbani R, Lix L, McClement S, et al. The impact of early palliative care on the quality of life of patients with advanced pancreatic cancer: The IMPERATIVE case-crossover study. Support Care Cancer. 2023;31(4):250.
SUPP-030.clinical_status: ASCO 2024 guideline: refer patients with advanced cancer to palliative care early, concurrent with treatment; checked 2026-10-08
SUPP-030.design: Prospective single-arm case-crossover; palliative care consultation within 2 weeks, visits q2w for a month then q4w to week 16; primary outcome FACT-Hep change baseline to week 16; ESAS-r, HADS, PHQ-9
SUPP-030.population: 40 ambulatory patients with advanced pancreatic cancer at a Canadian tertiary cancer centre (70% metastatic; 78% ECOG 0-1; 78% on chemotherapy; median age 70)
SUPP-030.finding: FACT-Hep 118.8 to 125.7 (mean change +6.89, 95% CI -1.69 to 15.6; P=0.11). Metastatic disease (+15.3, 5.3-25.2; P=0.004) and age <70 (+12.9) associated with QoL improvement; symptom burden fell in metastatic patients (ESAS -7.4, -13.4 to -1.4; P=0.02); no change in depression or anxiety (Results; Tables 1-4).
SUPP-030.effect: Primary endpoint not significant; metastatic subgroup +15.3 FACT-Hep
SUPP-030.limitations: Small; no randomization; pancreatic-specific RCT (Maltoni 2016, n=207) is paywalled: systematic early palliative care improved FACT-Hep TOI by 3.83 points (95% CI 0.10-7.57; P=0.041) with no survival difference (abstract lead)
SUPP-030.interpretation: Uncontrolled: cannot separate palliative care effect from chemotherapy response or attrition

glosses.fatigue: A Canadian prospective study found early palliative care lowered symptom burden in people with metastatic pancreatic cancer.
glosses.mood-support: A Canadian prospective study found early palliative care lowered symptom burden in metastatic disease but did not change depression or anxiety scores.
glosses.palliative-care: A Canadian prospective study of 40 people found early palliative care improved quality of life in metastatic disease and lowered symptom burden.

SUPP-031.citation: Gikandi A, Fong ZV, Qadan M, Narayan RR, Lwin T, Fernández-Del Castillo C, et al. Do Complications After Pancreatoduodenectomy Have an Impact on Long-Term Quality of Life and Functional Outcomes? Ann Surg Open. 2024;5(2):e400.
SUPP-031.design: Cross-sectional survey (EORTC QLQ-C30 and QLQ-PAN26) of long-term survivors stratified by index-admission complications; clinical-relevance thresholds
SUPP-031.population: 248 of 305 contactable patients surviving >5 years after pancreatoduodenectomy at Massachusetts General Hospital (231 with complication data; 29% had an index complication)
SUPP-031.finding: Global health status and functional scales similar between groups. Patients with complications reported lower fatigue (21.4 vs 28.1), diarrhea (15.9 vs 23.1), pancreatic pain (38.2 vs 43.4; small clinical relevance) and altered bowel habit (30.1 vs 40.7; moderate) scores; worrying 36.2% vs 60.5% and bloating 42.0% vs 56.2% (P<0.05) (Results; Tables 1-2). Persisting symptom burden >5 years after PD: pancreatic pain score ~40, altered bowel habits 30-41, bloating ~50%.
SUPP-031.effect: Global QoL difference nil; symptom scores differ by 5-10 points
SUPP-031.limitations: Non-responders 19%; benign and malignant indications mixed; no preoperative baseline
SUPP-031.interpretation: Cross-sectional survivor sample: describes long-term symptom load after Whipple; complication effect not causal (survivor and response bias)

glosses.fatigue: A survey of five-year Whipple survivors found modest fatigue scores and normal-range global quality of life.
glosses.life-after-whipple: A survey of 248 five-year Whipple survivors found normal-range global quality of life with persistent pancreatic pain and bowel symptoms.
glosses.stomach: Survey of Whipple survivors five or more years after surgery showing normal overall quality of life with persistent bowel symptoms.
glosses.whipple: A survey of 248 five-year Whipple survivors showing normal-range global quality of life with persistent pancreatic pain and bowel symptoms.
glosses.surgical-complications: A survey of 248 five-year Whipple survivors showing that early complications did not reduce long-term quality of life.

SUPP-032.citation: Sousa MS, Garcia MV, Blanchard M, Daveson B, Currow D, Khan NN, et al. Navigating pain and appetite challenges in palliative care for pancreatic cancer: insights from a national, longitudinal consecutive cohort study. Support Care Cancer. 2025;33(5):365.
SUPP-032.design: National consecutive point-of-care cohort; patient-reported symptom distress (SAS) and clinician ratings; logistic regression for associations; temporal trends
SUPP-032.population: 15,536 people with pancreatic cancer in 20,558 care episodes across 203 Australian specialist palliative care services (Palliative Care Outcomes Collaboration), 2013-2022
SUPP-032.finding: At admission to palliative care, 69% reported distress from pain and 60% from appetite; among those with pain or appetite distress, co-occurring distress for sleep (79%/82%), nausea (83%/85%), bowels (80%/83%), breathing (70%/77%), fatigue (77%/77%). Appetite distress associated with psychological/spiritual problems (inpatient OR 1.78, 1.66-1.90) and pain severity (community OR 1.51); pain distress with pain severity (inpatient OR 1.60, 1.49-1.72). Over the decade, mild appetite distress rose +10% while moderate (-22%) and severe (-11%) fell, with similar trends for pain (Results; Tables 1-5).
SUPP-032.effect: Pain distress 69%, appetite distress 60% at palliative-care referral
SUPP-032.limitations: Not stage-stratified at diagnosis; Australian services
SUPP-032.interpretation: Descriptive prevalence at the palliative stage (late-stage boundary of the pain-prevalence question); associations observational

glosses.pain: A national Australian cohort of 15,536 people with pancreatic cancer found 69% reported pain distress at palliative-care admission, usually with sleep, nausea and bowel distress.
glosses.fatigue: A national Australian cohort found fatigue distress in 77% of people with pain or appetite distress at palliative-care admission.
glosses.mood-support: A national Australian cohort of 15,536 people found appetite distress linked to psychological and spiritual problems and symptoms clustering together.
glosses.palliative-care: A national Australian cohort of 15,536 people with pancreatic cancer documented pain, appetite and clustered symptom distress at palliative-care admission.

SUPP-033.citation: Aydın O, Korkmaz YY, Altay M, Kudaş İ, Baş S, Bostancı Ö, et al. New-Onset Diabetes After Pancreaticoduodenectomy: 3D Volumetric Analysis and Evaluation of Preoperative Metabolic Load. J Clin Med. 2026;15(17):6693.
SUPP-033.design: Retrospective cohort; 3D CT volumetry (total pancreas volume, remnant volume, 6-month atrophy rate, indexed to body weight); multivariable logistic regression and ROC for NODM
SUPP-033.population: 159 non-diabetic patients undergoing pancreaticoduodenectomy at a Turkish centre with preoperative and 6-month CT
SUPP-033.finding: NODM 48/159 (30.2%) by 6-month follow-up. No significant difference between NODM and non-NODM groups in weight-indexed total pancreas volume, preoperative remnant volume or postoperative atrophy rate (P=0.475). BMI was the sole independent predictor (OR 1.125 per unit, P=0.006); BMI >26.5 kg/m2 AUC 0.644 (Results; Tables 1-4).
SUPP-033.interpretation: Observational contradiction of the remnant-volume paradigm for NODM after PD; supports metabolic load as determinant

glosses.glucose-diabetes: A Turkish series of 159 Whipple patients found new diabetes in 30% by six months, predicted by body-mass index rather than remnant volume.
glosses.life-after-whipple: A Turkish series of 159 Whipple patients found new diabetes in 30% by six months, predicted by body-mass index rather than remnant volume.
glosses.pancreas-body-tail: Volumetric study showing body-mass index, not remnant pancreas volume, predicted new diabetes after a Whipple.
glosses.spleen: Volumetric study showing body-mass index, not remnant pancreas volume, predicted new diabetes after a Whipple.
glosses.whipple: A Turkish series of 159 Whipple patients with new diabetes in 30% by six months, predicted by body-mass index rather than remnant volume.
glosses.diabetes-after-surgery: A Turkish cohort of 159 people after a Whipple in which 30 percent had new diabetes by six months, predicted by body-mass index but not by CT-measured remnant volume.

SUPP-034.citation: Yun SP, Seo HI, Kim S, Kim DU, Baek DH. Does the pancreatic volume reduction rate using serial computed tomographic volumetry predict new onset diabetes after pancreaticoduodenectomy? Medicine (Baltimore). 2017;96(13):e6491.
SUPP-034.design: Retrospective cohort with protocolized serial CT volumetry; NODM vs normal glucose groups; multivariable logistic regression; ROC for 6-month volume reduction rate
SUPP-034.population: 66 non-diabetic patients undergoing pancreaticoduodenectomy for periampullary tumors in Busan, Korea, Aug 2007-Dec 2012, with serial CT at 7 days, 6, 12, 24 and 36 months
SUPP-034.finding: NODM in 16/66 (24.2%), most frequent with advanced T-stage carcinoma. Volume reduction rate at 6 and 12 months higher in NODM group (univariate); at multivariable analysis the 6-month reduction rate was the only independent predictor (P=0.002); ROC cut-off 64% reduction at 6 months: AUC 0.809, sensitivity 0.750, specificity 0.776 (Tables 3-4; Figure 2).
SUPP-034.limitations: Small; single centre; no metabolic covariates such as BMI/HbA1c modeled in accessed text
SUPP-034.interpretation: Observational support for the atrophy -> diabetes model after PD (independent of SUPP-033's null)

glosses.diabetes-after-surgery: A Korean cohort of 66 people with serial CT after a Whipple in which shrinkage of the remnant by 64 percent or more at six months predicted new diabetes.

SUPP-035.citation: Ishido K, Fujita H, Kimura N, Nagase H, Wakasa Y, Tsuruta S, et al. Significance of Pancreatic Steatosis as a Predictor of New-Onset Diabetes Mellitus Following Pancreatectomy. Pancreas. 2025;54(9):e765-e775.
SUPP-035.design: Retrospective cohort; anticipated remnant pancreas-to-spleen CT attenuation ratio (remP/S; lower = more fat) and remnant volume; Kaplan-Meier time to diabetes; Cox regression; risk score
SUPP-035.population: 220 non-diabetic patients undergoing pancreatoduodenectomy or distal pancreatectomy at Hirosaki University Hospital, 2008-2020, follow-up >=6 months
SUPP-035.finding: NODM 7.2% at 1 year, 21.3% at 3 years, 28.0% at 5 years (median follow-up 25.1 months). Univariate risks: pancreatic cancer, HbA1c >5.7%, remP/S <0.66, PNI <50, remnant volume <32.7 cm3. Multivariable: remP/S <0.66 and HbA1c >5.7% independent; both factors -> ~5-fold risk of NODM within 2 years vs neither (Results; Tables 1-2).
SUPP-035.effect: Steatosis + prediabetic HbA1c: ~5x NODM at 2 years
SUPP-035.interpretation: Observational: a tissue-quality (fat) and baseline-metabolic determinant that outperforms crude remnant volume; discriminates between the two competing explanations by combining them

glosses.glucose-diabetes: A Japanese series of 220 resections found a fatty remnant plus borderline HbA1c multiplied new-diabetes risk about fivefold.
glosses.life-after-whipple: A Japanese series of 220 resections found diabetes risk rising over years, driven by a fatty remnant and borderline HbA1c.
glosses.diabetes-after-surgery: A Japanese cohort of 220 people after partial pancreatectomy in which a fatty remnant on CT and a pre-operative HbA1c above 5.7 percent together gave about five times the risk of diabetes.

SUPP-036.citation: Maiga I, Vilotitch A, Genoux B, Chirica M, Girard E, Bétry C. Malnutrition and diabetes outcomes 12 months after total pancreatectomy: A descriptive cohort study. JPEN J Parenter Enteral Nutr. 2026;50(4):573-581.
SUPP-036.clinical_status: Insulin therapy standard after total pancreatectomy; CGM and pumps FDA-approved devices; bihormonal artificial pancreas investigational (PANORAMA crossover RCT protocol, BJS Open 2025); checked 2026-10-08
SUPP-036.design: Prospective descriptive cohort; nutrition status (French criteria: weight loss, BMI, CT muscle mass or function) preoperatively, 3 and 12 months; diabetes control at 12 months by HbA1c and continuous glucose monitoring (time in range, time below range)
SUPP-036.population: 41 adults undergoing total pancreatectomy at Grenoble Alpes University Hospital, Jan 2021-Jul 2024 (benign and malignant indications)
SUPP-036.finding: Malnutrition 25.0% (95% CI 12.7-41.2) preoperatively vs 59.5% (42.1-75.2) at 3 months and 59.0% (42.1-74.4) at 12 months; >10% weight loss in more than half at 12 months. All patients had type 3c diabetes immediately after surgery; at 12 months median HbA1c 8.0% (IQR 7.2-8.8; n=32) on multiple daily injections or pump; median time below range (<70 mg/dL) 0.2% (0.0-1.5) (Results; Tables 1-3).
SUPP-036.limitations: Single centre; mixed indications; insulin dose data not in accessed text
SUPP-036.interpretation: Boundary condition: complete removal yields deterministic insulin-dependent diabetes; shows glycaemia is manageable with low hypoglycaemia but nutrition deteriorates

glosses.glucose-diabetes: A French cohort of 41 total pancreatectomies found universal insulin-requiring diabetes with median HbA1c 8.0% and little hypoglycemia at one year.
glosses.nutrition: A French cohort of 41 total pancreatectomies found malnutrition in 59% at one year despite follow-up.
glosses.life-after-whipple: A French cohort of 41 total pancreatectomies found universal insulin-requiring diabetes and malnutrition in 59% at one year.
glosses.pancreas-overview: French cohort showing universal insulin-requiring diabetes and persistent malnutrition one year after total pancreatectomy.
glosses.islets: French cohort showing universal insulin-requiring diabetes and persistent malnutrition one year after total pancreatectomy.
glosses.total-pancreatectomy: A French prospective cohort of 41 total pancreatectomies: universal diabetes, HbA1c 8.0% at one year, and malnutrition in 59%.
glosses.diabetes-after-surgery: A French prospective cohort of 41 people after total pancreatectomy, all insulin-dependent, with a median HbA1c of 8.0 percent and very little hypoglycemia at one year but malnutrition in 59 percent.

SUPP-L01.citation: Bruno MJ, Haverkort EB, Tijssen GP, Tytgat GN, van Leeuwen DJ. Placebo controlled trial of enteric coated pancreatin microsphere treatment in patients with unresectable cancer of the pancreatic head region. Gut. 1998;42(1):92-96.
SUPP-L01.design: Randomized double-blind placebo-controlled 8-week trial of high-dose enteric-coated pancreatin plus dietary counselling
SUPP-L01.population: 21 patients with unresectable pancreatic head-region cancer, biliary stent in situ, Karnofsky >60
SUPP-L01.finding: Abstract: weight change difference 4.9% (95% CI 0.9-8.9; P=0.02): +1.2% (0.7 kg) on enzymes vs -3.7% (-2.2 kg) placebo; fat absorption +12% vs -8% (P=0.13); energy intake 8.42 vs 6.66 MJ/day (P=0.04).
SUPP-L01.limitations: Full text not retrievable in this environment
SUPP-L01.interpretation: Abstract-level only; not used as counted evidence

glosses.weight-loss-cachexia: A 1998 placebo-controlled trial of enzyme capsules in unresectable pancreatic cancer found weight +1.2% versus -3.7% over eight weeks (abstract only).
glosses.digestion-enzymes: A 1998 placebo-controlled trial of enzyme capsules in unresectable pancreatic cancer found weight +1.2% versus -3.7% over eight weeks (abstract only).
glosses.nutrition: A 1998 placebo-controlled trial of enzyme capsules in unresectable pancreatic cancer found weight +1.2% versus -3.7% over eight weeks (abstract only).
glosses.enzyme-replacement: A 1998 placebo-controlled trial, known here from its abstract, in which 21 people with unresectable pancreatic head cancer gained weight on enzymes while the placebo group lost it.

SUPP-L02.citation: Fearon KC, Von Meyenfeldt MF, Moses AG, et al. Effect of a protein and energy dense N-3 fatty acid enriched oral supplement on loss of weight and lean tissue in cancer cachexia: a randomised double blind trial. Gut. 2003;52(10):1479-1486.
SUPP-L02.design: Multicentre double-blind RCT, EPA-enriched vs isocaloric isonitrogenous supplement, 8 weeks
SUPP-L02.population: 200 cachectic patients with advanced pancreatic cancer
SUPP-L02.finding: Abstract: both groups stopped losing weight (delta -0.25 vs -0.37 kg/month; P=0.74) and lean mass; mean intake 1.4 of 2 cans/day; post hoc dose-response for EPA arm (r=0.50 for weight).
SUPP-L02.limitations: Full text not retrievable in this environment
SUPP-L02.interpretation: Abstract-level only; not used as counted evidence

glosses.weight-loss-cachexia: A 2003 randomized trial of an omega-3-enriched protein supplement in pancreatic cancer found weight loss stopped in both arms (abstract only).
glosses.nutrition: A 2003 randomized trial of an omega-3-enriched protein supplement in pancreatic cancer found weight loss stopped in both arms (abstract only).
glosses.enzyme-replacement: A 2003 randomized trial in 200 people with pancreatic cancer cachexia, known here from its abstract, in which an omega-3-enriched and a standard supplement halted weight loss equally.
glosses.cachexia-treatments: A 2003 randomized trial in 200 people with pancreatic cancer cachexia, known here from its abstract, in which an omega-3-enriched and a standard supplement halted weight loss equally.

SUPP-L03.citation: Wigmore SJ, Plester CE, Richardson RA, Fearon KC. Changes in nutritional status associated with unresectable pancreatic cancer. Br J Cancer. 1997;75(1):106-109.
SUPP-L03.population: 20 patients with unresectable pancreatic cancer followed monthly to death
SUPP-L03.finding: Abstract: all 20 had lost weight at diagnosis, median 14.2% (IQR 10-20) of pre-illness weight, progressing to 24.5% before death; BMI 24.9 -> 20.7 -> 17.7; lean mass 43.4 -> 40.1 kg; fat 12.5 -> 9.6 kg.
SUPP-L03.limitations: Full text not retrievable in this environment
SUPP-L03.interpretation: Abstract-level only; not used as counted evidence

glosses.weight-loss-cachexia: A 1997 study of 20 people with unresectable pancreatic cancer documented a median 14% weight loss at diagnosis progressing to 24.5% (abstract only).

SUPP-L04.citation: Wyse JM, Carone M, Paquin SC, Usatii M, Sahai AV. Randomized, double-blind, controlled trial of early endoscopic ultrasound-guided celiac plexus neurolysis to prevent pain progression in patients with newly diagnosed, painful, inoperable pancreatic cancer. J Clin Oncol. 2011;29(26):3541-3546.
SUPP-L04.design: Double-blind RCT early EUS-CPN vs conventional pain management
SUPP-L04.population: 96 patients with newly diagnosed painful inoperable pancreatic adenocarcinoma at diagnostic EUS
SUPP-L04.finding: Abstract: difference in mean % change in pain score -28.9 (95% CI -67.0 to 2.8; P=0.09) at 1 month and -60.7 (-86.6 to -25.5; P=0.01) at 3 months; morphine difference -49.5 (-127.5 to 7.0; P=0.10) at 3 months; no effect on QoL or survival.
SUPP-L04.limitations: Full text not retrievable in this environment
SUPP-L04.interpretation: Abstract-level only; not used as counted evidence

glosses.pain: A randomized trial of early endoscopic ultrasound-guided celiac neurolysis found a 60.7% greater fall in pain at three months (abstract only).
glosses.nerve-plexus: Abstract of a randomized trial showing early endoscopic celiac plexus neurolysis reduced pain at three months.

SUPP-L05.citation: Levy MJ, Gleeson FC, Topazian MD, et al. Combined Celiac Ganglia and Plexus Neurolysis Shortens Survival, Without Benefit, vs Plexus Neurolysis Alone. Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2019;17(4):728-738.e9.
SUPP-L05.design: Randomized double-blind EUS-CPN (n=60) vs celiac ganglia neurolysis (n=50)
SUPP-L05.population: 110 patients with unresectable PDAC and abdominal pain (Mayo)
SUPP-L05.finding: Abstract: pain response at 12 weeks 46.2% CGN vs 40.4% CPN (P=0.84); median survival 5.59 vs 10.46 months, HR 1.49 (1.02-2.19; P=0.042) for CGN, HR 2.95 in non-metastatic disease; 12-month survival 26% vs 42%.
SUPP-L05.limitations: Full text not retrievable in this environment
SUPP-L05.interpretation: Abstract-level only; not used as counted evidence

glosses.pain: A randomized comparison found adding celiac ganglia neurolysis to plexus neurolysis shortened survival without better pain relief (abstract only).
glosses.nerve-plexus: Abstract reporting that adding celiac ganglia neurolysis to plexus neurolysis shortened survival without extra pain benefit.

SUPP-L06.citation: Kanno Y, Koshita S, Masu K, et al. Efficacy of EUS-guided celiac plexus neurolysis compared with medication alone for unresectable pancreatic cancer in the oxycodone/fentanyl era: a prospective randomized control study. Gastrointest Endosc. 2020;92(1):120-130.
SUPP-L06.design: RCT EUS-CPN plus medication vs medication alone; primary VAS at 4 weeks
SUPP-L06.population: 48 patients with pancreatic cancer pain on oxycodone/fentanyl
SUPP-L06.finding: Abstract: VAS at week 4 1.3+/-1.3 vs 2.3+/-2.3 (P=0.10); no difference in QoL or opioid consumption at any point; no severe procedure AEs.
SUPP-L06.limitations: Full text not retrievable in this environment
SUPP-L06.interpretation: Abstract-level only; not used as counted evidence

glosses.pain: A randomized trial of endoscopic neurolysis plus medication versus medication alone found no significant difference in pain at four weeks (abstract only).
glosses.nerve-plexus: Abstract of a randomized trial finding no pain difference between endoscopic celiac plexus neurolysis and medication alone.

SUPP-L07.citation: van der Gaag NA, Rauws EA, van Eijck CH, et al. Preoperative biliary drainage for cancer of the head of the pancreas. N Engl J Med. 2010;362(2):129-137.
SUPP-L07.design: Multicentre RCT: PBD (mostly plastic endoprosthesis) for 4-6 weeks then surgery vs surgery within 1 week
SUPP-L07.population: 202 patients with pancreatic head cancer and bilirubin 40-250 umol/L
SUPP-L07.finding: Abstract: serious complications within 120 days 39% vs 74% (RR 0.54 for early surgery, 95% CI 0.41-0.71; P<0.001); PBD complications 46%; surgery-related complications 37% vs 47% (P=0.14); mortality and stay similar.
SUPP-L07.limitations: Full text not retrievable in this environment
SUPP-L07.interpretation: Abstract-level only; not used as counted evidence

glosses.jaundice: The 2010 Dutch trial of preoperative drainage with plastic stents found more serious complications than with early surgery (abstract only).
glosses.obstruction-warning: The 2010 Dutch trial of preoperative drainage with plastic stents found more serious complications than with early surgery (abstract only).
glosses.bile-duct-ampulla: Abstract of the 2010 trial showing routine plastic-stent drainage before surgery increased complications compared with early surgery.
glosses.biliary-stents: The 2010 Dutch randomized trial, known here from its abstract, in which preoperative drainage with mostly plastic stents raised serious complications from 39 to 74 percent.

SUPP-L08.citation: Teoh AYB, Lakhtakia S, Tarantino I, et al. Endoscopic ultrasonography-guided gastroenterostomy versus uncovered duodenal metal stenting for unresectable malignant gastric outlet obstruction (DRA-GOO): a multicentre randomised controlled trial. Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2025;10(6):e8-e16 (corrected republication of the retracted 2024;9(2):124-132 article).
SUPP-L08.design: RCT EUS-GE (double-balloon occluder) vs duodenal stent; primary 6-month reintervention
SUPP-L08.population: 97 patients with malignant GOO (GOOS 0) at 7 sites
SUPP-L08.finding: Abstract (2025 corrected version): reintervention within 6 months 2 (4%) vs 14 (29%), RR 0.15 (0.04-0.61; P=0.002); 1-month GOOS 2.41 vs 1.91 (P=0.012); 30-day death 21% vs 12% (P=0.29); AEs 23% vs 24%. NOTE: the original 2024 paper was retracted and republished with corrections in 2025; the atlas should cite the 2025 version.
SUPP-L08.limitations: Full text not retrievable in this environment
SUPP-L08.interpretation: Abstract-level only; not used as counted evidence

glosses.obstruction-warning: The republished 2025 DRA-GOO trial found reintervention in 4% after endoscopic gastroenterostomy versus 29% after duodenal stenting (abstract only).

SUPP-L09.citation: Pelzer U, Opitz B, Deutschinoff G, et al. Efficacy of Prophylactic Low-Molecular Weight Heparin for Ambulatory Patients With Advanced Pancreatic Cancer: Outcomes From the CONKO-004 Trial. J Clin Oncol. 2015;33(18):2028-2034.
SUPP-L09.design: Open RCT enoxaparin (1 mg/kg daily x3 months then 40 mg) vs observation
SUPP-L09.population: 312 patients with advanced pancreatic cancer starting first-line chemotherapy
SUPP-L09.finding: Abstract: symptomatic VTE in first 3 months 2/160 vs 15/152 (HR 0.12, 0.03-0.52; P=0.001); overall cumulative symptomatic VTE 6.4% vs 15.1% (HR 0.40, 0.19-0.83); major bleeding 7 vs 5; PFS/OS unchanged.
SUPP-L09.limitations: Full text not retrievable in this environment
SUPP-L09.interpretation: Abstract-level only; not used as counted evidence

glosses.blood-clots: The CONKO-004 trial found prophylactic enoxaparin cut symptomatic clots in the first three months without changing survival (abstract only).
glosses.vte-prevention: The CONKO-004 randomized trial of enoxaparin versus observation in 312 people with advanced pancreatic cancer, known here from its abstract, which reduced symptomatic clots without changing survival.

SUPP-L10.citation: Maltoni M, Scarpi E, Dall'Agata M, et al. Systematic versus on-demand early palliative care: results from a multicentre, randomised clinical trial. Eur J Cancer. 2016;65:61-68.
SUPP-L10.design: RCT systematic early palliative care vs on-demand; primary FACT-Hep TOI change at 12 weeks
SUPP-L10.population: 207 outpatients with metastatic or locally advanced inoperable pancreatic cancer (Italy)
SUPP-L10.finding: Abstract: TOI difference 3.83 (95% CI 0.10-7.57; P=0.041) and HCS difference 2.51 (0.40-4.61; P=0.013) favouring systematic EPC; no OS difference; 76.9% died by Feb 2016.
SUPP-L10.limitations: Full text not retrievable in this environment
SUPP-L10.interpretation: Abstract-level only; not used as counted evidence

glosses.mood-support: A multicenter randomized trial found systematic early palliative care modestly improved quality of life in pancreatic cancer without changing survival (abstract only).
glosses.palliative-care: A multicenter randomized trial of 207 people found systematic early palliative care modestly improved quality of life in pancreatic cancer without changing survival (abstract only).

SUPP-L11.citation: Frere C, Bournet B, Gourgou S, et al. Incidence of Venous Thromboembolism in Patients With Newly Diagnosed Pancreatic Cancer and Factors Associated With Outcomes. Gastroenterology. 2020;158(5):1346-1358.e4.
SUPP-L11.finding: Abstract: VTE 20.79% at median 19.3 months; cumulative 8.07% at 3 and 19.21% at 12 months; isthmus location HR 2.06; metastatic HR 2.50; VTE -> OS HR 2.02 (1.57-2.60).
SUPP-L11.limitations: Full text not retrievable in this environment
SUPP-L11.interpretation: Abstract-level only; not used as counted evidence

glosses.blood-clots: The parent French cohort paper found clots in 21% over follow-up and associated them with shorter survival (abstract only).
glosses.vte-prevention: The parent BACAP cohort report of 731 people, known here from its abstract, in which clots were more frequent with metastatic disease and neck-of-pancreas tumors and doubled the hazard of death.

SUPP-L12.citation: Wiskemann J, Clauss D, Tjaden C, et al. Progressive Resistance Training to Impact Physical Fitness and Body Weight in Pancreatic Cancer Patients: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Pancreas. 2019;48(2):257-266.
SUPP-L12.design: 3-arm RCT supervised vs home resistance training vs usual care, 6 months
SUPP-L12.finding: Abstract: adherence 64.1% supervised, 78.4% home; supervised training improved elbow flexor/extensor strength and maximal workload vs control and home (P<0.05), knee extensors vs control; no body-weight differences.
SUPP-L12.limitations: Full text not retrievable in this environment
SUPP-L12.interpretation: Abstract-level only; not used as counted evidence

glosses.fatigue: A German randomized trial found supervised resistance training improved strength without changing body weight (abstract only).
glosses.activity-function: A German randomized trial found supervised resistance training improved strength without changing body weight (abstract only).

SUPP-L13.citation: Kwak BJ, Choi HJ, You YK, Kim DG, Hong TH. Comparative long-term outcomes for pancreatic volume change, nutritional status, and incidence of new-onset diabetes between pancreatogastrostomy and pancreatojejunostomy after pancreaticoduodenectomy. Hepatobiliary Surg Nutr. 2020;9(3):284-295.
SUPP-L13.design: Retrospective comparison PG vs PJ with 5-year serial volumetry
SUPP-L13.population: 115 >3-year survivors after PD (88 non-diabetic for NODM analysis)
SUPP-L13.finding: Abstract: volume reduction -18.2 vs -14.4 mL (P=0.21); duct dilation greater after PG (1.66 vs 0.54 mm; P=0.007); nutritional indices similar; NODM analysis in 88 patients (details not in abstract).
SUPP-L13.limitations: Full text not retrievable in this environment
SUPP-L13.interpretation: Abstract-level only; not used as counted evidence

RAS-001.citation: Strickler JH, Satake H, George TJ, Yaeger R, Hollebecque A, Garrido-Laguna I, et al. Sotorasib in KRAS p.G12C-Mutated Advanced Pancreatic Cancer. N Engl J Med. 2023;388(1):33-43.
RAS-001.clinical_status: Sotorasib has no US pancreatic indication; US label covers KRAS G12C NSCLC (accelerated approval) and, with panitumumab, KRAS G12C mCRC. Checked 2026-10-08.
RAS-001.design: Single-arm phase 1 (dose finding, n=12) plus phase 2 (n=26) pancreatic cohorts of CodeBreaK 100, pooled for efficacy; primary phase 2 endpoint centrally confirmed objective response (BICR)
RAS-001.population: Adults with metastatic KRAS p.G12C-mutated pancreatic cancer, >=1 prior systemic therapy; median 2 prior lines (range 1-8); 11% ECOG 2
RAS-001.n: 38 patients treated (12 phase 1 + 26 phase 2); 25 centres in 7 countries
RAS-001.time_frame: Enrolment 3 July 2019 - 25 January 2021; median follow-up 16.8 mo (95% CI 9.5-NE); median treatment duration 18 weeks (range 1-48)
RAS-001.finding: Confirmed objective response 8/38 = 21% (95% CI 10-37), all partial; disease control 84% (95% CI 69-94); any-magnitude tumour shrinkage in 30/38 (79%); median time to response 1.5 mo (range 1.3-5.6); median duration of response 5.7 mo (95% CI 1.6-NE) (Table 2); median PFS 4.0 mo (95% CI 2.8-5.6), KM PFS 31.6% (16.7-47.7) at 6 mo and 9.9% (2.0-25.6) at 9 mo (Fig 1C); median OS 6.9 mo (95% CI 5.0-9.1), 12-mo OS 19.6% (7.2-36.3) (Fig 1D); treatment-related AEs any grade 16/38 (42%), grade 3 6/38 (16%), none grade 4-5, none causing discontinuation; all-cause grade >=3 AEs 24/38 (63%); 14/38 (37%) had fatal events, none treatment-attributed (Table 3)
RAS-001.effect: ORR 21%; median DoR 5.7 mo; median PFS 4.0 mo; median OS 6.9 mo
RAS-001.limitations: n=38, single arm, no randomisation; KRAS G12C is a rare PDAC allele so the cohort is not representative; duration of response not estimable per phase; 37% died during follow-up.
RAS-001.interpretation: Single-arm biomarker-selected trial: establishes that pharmacological inhibition of a specific KRAS allele produces measurable tumour shrinkage in human PDAC, but cannot attribute survival to the drug and cannot show durability.

glosses.kras-alleles-wildtype: The 38-patient sotorasib trial in KRAS G12C pancreatic cancer, confirmed response 21 percent, median survival 6.9 months.
glosses.kras-g12c-inhibitors: The CodeBreaK 100 pancreatic cohort: 38 previously treated patients with KRAS G12C tumors took sotorasib, 21 percent had a confirmed response and median survival was 6.9 months.

RAS-002.citation: Bekaii-Saab TS, Yaeger R, Spira AI, Pelster MS, Sabari JK, Hafez N, et al. Adagrasib in Advanced Solid Tumors Harboring a KRAS(G12C) Mutation. J Clin Oncol. 2023;41(25):4097-4106.
RAS-002.clinical_status: Adagrasib has no US pancreatic indication; US label covers KRAS G12C NSCLC and, with cetuximab, KRAS G12C CRC, both accelerated approvals. Checked 2026-10-08.
RAS-002.design: Open-label single-arm phase 2 cohort of KRYSTAL-1 (phase Ib/II basket), predictive-probability futility design; primary endpoint ORR by RECIST v1.1 (BICR)
RAS-002.population: Adults with KRAS G12C-mutated unresectable/metastatic solid tumours excluding NSCLC and CRC; median 2 prior lines; KRAS G12C determined in tumour tissue (PCR, NeoGenomics) or ctDNA (Resolution Bioscience NGS)
RAS-002.n: 64 enrolled, 63 treated; 57 with measurable disease at baseline; pancreatic subgroup n=21, biliary tract n=12
RAS-002.time_frame: Enrolment March 2020 - September 2022 (30 months); data cutoff 1 October 2022; median follow-up 16.8 mo
RAS-002.finding: ORR 20/57 = 35.1%, all partial responses; pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma 7/21 = 33.3%; biliary tract 5/12 = 41.7%; median time to response 1.4 mo; median duration of response 5.3 mo (95% CI 2.8-7.3) by BICR and 7.0 mo (95% CI 3.1-9.9) by investigator (Fig 2B-C); median PFS 7.4 mo (95% CI 5.3-8.6) by BICR in the 57 measurable patients and 6.9 mo (5.3-8.3) by investigator in all 63; median OS 14.0 mo (95% CI 8.5-NE); treatment-related AEs any grade 96.8%, grade 3-4 27.0%, no grade 5, no TRAE-related discontinuations; 14 patients still on treatment at cutoff. The paper states KRAS G12C occurs in 1%-3% of pancreatic cancers.
RAS-002.effect: Pancreatic ORR 33.3% (7/21); overall ORR 35.1%; median DoR 5.3 mo
RAS-002.limitations: Single arm; pancreatic-specific PFS/OS not reported in the main text (later cited elsewhere as 5.4 and 8.0 months); BICR-versus-investigator DoR differ by ~1.7 months; shares the KRYSTAL-1 trial with RAS-006 and RAS-015 though different patient cohorts.
RAS-002.interpretation: Prospective biomarker-selected single-arm cohort; supports drug-attributable tumour shrinkage across tumour types sharing one allele, i.e. a largely tumour-agnostic target effect.

glosses.kras-alleles-wildtype: The adagrasib basket cohort in which 7 of 21 pancreatic patients responded; states G12C occurs in 1 to 3 percent of pancreatic cancers.
glosses.kras-g12c-inhibitors: The KRYSTAL-1 basket cohort of adagrasib in non-lung, non-colorectal KRAS G12C tumors, in which 7 of 21 pancreatic patients responded for a median of 5.3 months.

RAS-003.citation: Holderfield M, Lee BJ, Jiang J, Tomlinson A, Seamon KJ, Mira A, et al. Concurrent inhibition of oncogenic and wild-type RAS-GTP for cancer therapy. Nature. 2024;629(8013):919-926.
RAS-003.clinical_status: RMC-7977 is a preclinical tool compound only; the clinical analogue RMC-6236 (daraxonrasib) is now US-approved for mPDAC. Checked 2026-10-08.
RAS-003.design: Preclinical pharmacology: biochemistry/structure of a reversible tri-complex RAS(ON) multi-selective inhibitor (RMC-7977), cell-line panel sensitivity, PK/PD, in vivo 'mouse clinical trial' across 15 models, and direct comparison with SHP2 (RMC-4550) and MEK (cobimetinib) inhibition
RAS-003.population: Human cancer cell lines (PRISM/CRISPR dependency data), cell-line-derived xenografts (CDX) and patient-derived xenografts (PDX) of PDAC, CRC and NSCLC bearing KRAS codon-12 (KRAS G12X) mutations; mice
RAS-003.n: 15 CDX/PDX models bearing KRAS G12X across PDAC, CRC and NSCLC; cell-line panels; 3 models for the vertical-pathway comparison
RAS-003.time_frame: 4-6 week primary treatment periods; durability assessed to 90 days
RAS-003.finding: Repeated daily RMC-7977 at 10 mg/kg gave 83% mean tumour regression after 28 days in NCI-H441 (Fig 3d). Across the 15-model KRAS G12X CDX/PDX panel, mean tumour regression occurred in 9/15 (60%) after 4-6 weeks of treatment with minimal body-weight effect (Fig 3e; Extended Data Fig 8c). With dosing continued up to 90 days, regressions and cytostatic responses were largely maintained: control tumours had a median time to tumour doubling of 7 days whereas RMC-7977-treated tumours did not reach median time to doubling (Fig 3f; Cox HR 0.004, 95% interval 0.0011-0.0191, P<1x10^-12). In three KRAS G12X models RMC-7977 induced deep regressions whereas MEK and SHP2 inhibitors alone or combined produced only modest growth inhibition (Fig 3g). RMC-7977 also inhibited growth of KRAS G12C models resistant to G12C inhibitors through restored RAS pathway signalling.
RAS-003.effect: 60% (9/15) of KRAS G12X models regressed; HR for tumour doubling 0.004 (95% interval 0.0011-0.0191)
RAS-003.limitations: RMC-7977 is a tool compound, not the clinical agent (daraxonrasib/RMC-6236); mouse exposures and tolerability do not transfer directly; no autochthonous immunocompetent model in the key comparison.
RAS-003.interpretation: Perturbation experiment with a matched-potency comparator arm: isolates the causal contribution of targeting active RAS itself versus targeting the pathway above (SHP2) or below (MEK) it.

glosses.daraxonrasib: The preclinical study in which a multi-selective RAS(ON) inhibitor regressed 9 of 15 KRAS-mutant tumor models and outperformed SHP2 and MEK inhibition.
glosses.ras-on-inhibitors: The Nature paper on the tool compound RMC-7977, in which 9 of 15 KRAS-mutant mouse tumor models regressed and active-state RAS inhibition outperformed SHP2 and MEK inhibitors head to head.

RAS-004.citation: Kemp SB, Cheng N, Markosyan N, Sor R, Kim IK, Hallin J, et al. Efficacy of a Small-Molecule Inhibitor of KrasG12D in Immunocompetent Models of Pancreatic Cancer. Cancer Discov. 2023;13(2):298-311.
RAS-004.clinical_status: MRTX1133 preclinical; its first-in-human phase 1 (NCT05737706) was terminated for 'Formulation challenges' with 63 patients enrolled (registry checked 2026-10-08). No KRAS G12D-selective inhibitor is US-approved.
RAS-004.design: Randomised preclinical intervention with antibody-mediated T-cell depletion as the mechanistic test; flow cytometry, immunofluorescence, cytokine profiling of the tumour microenvironment
RAS-004.population: Syngeneic C57BL/6 mice bearing KrasG12D PDAC lines (6419c5, 2838c3) subcutaneously and orthotopically, and the autochthonous KPC/Y (KrasLSL-G12D/+; Trp53LSL-R172H/+; p48-Cre; YFP lineage label) mouse model
RAS-004.n: Subcutaneous 6419c5 n=10/group; 2838c3 n=7-8/group; orthotopic n=5-6/group; autochthonous KPC/Y n=13-14/group; TME flow cytometry n=15-16/group
RAS-004.time_frame: 7-day and 14-day treatment; TME changes at 60 h and day 7
RAS-004.finding: Subcutaneous 6419c5: tumour volume separated by day 2; after 7 days 5/10 (50%) tumours regressed and 5/10 had static or modest growth (Fig 1A; Supplementary Fig S2A-B). Orthotopic (ultrasound-guided) 6419c5: regressions in 6/6 (100%) after 7 days, but no complete responses (Fig 1C). Autochthonous KPC/Y: after 14 days regressions in 12/13 (92%) treated animals, 4 with tumour below the ultrasound limit of detection (Fig 4B). T-cell depletion: tumours in the MRTX1133 + anti-CD4/CD8 arm showed substantial regrowth after an initial response (Fig 3C-D). TME: after 5 doses over 60 h, significant increases in intratumoral CD3+, CD4+ and CD8+ T cells with higher Ki-67 and granzyme B on CD8+ T cells (Fig 2G-H), reduced granulocytic MDSCs, increased M1-like macrophages, and increased IFN-gamma+ CD8+ T cells in tumour-draining lymph nodes (Fig 2I); the T-cell infiltration increase was no longer…
RAS-004.effect: 92% (12/13) regression in autochthonous tumours at 14 days; loss of durable control on T-cell depletion
RAS-004.limitations: Mouse PDAC models carry lower mutational burden diversity and are not immunotherapy-matched to human disease; MRTX1133 requires parenteral dosing; short treatment durations; the T-cell influx is transient and its mechanism is unexplained.
RAS-004.interpretation: Depletion (loss-of-function) experiment inside an immunocompetent and autochthonous model: supports a necessary role for T cells in sustaining, not initiating, the response to KRAS G12D inhibition.

glosses.kras-g12d-inhibitors: A mouse study in which the G12D inhibitor MRTX1133 regressed 12 of 13 spontaneous pancreatic tumors, with T cells shown to be required to prevent regrowth.
glosses.ras-resistance: The mouse study of a KRAS G12D drug in which 12 of 13 spontaneous pancreatic tumors regressed, T cells entered the tumor transiently, and removing T cells allowed regrowth.

RAS-005.citation: Chung V, McDonough S, Philip PA, Cardin D, Wang-Gillam A, Hui L, et al. Effect of Selumetinib and MK-2206 vs Oxaliplatin and Fluorouracil in Patients With Metastatic Pancreatic Cancer After Prior Therapy: SWOG S1115 Study Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Oncol. 2017;3(4):516-522.
RAS-005.clinical_status: Negative randomised phase 2; neither selumetinib nor MK-2206 is approved for pancreatic cancer in the US. Checked 2026-10-08.
RAS-005.design: Randomised (1:1) open-label phase 2 cooperative-group trial stratified by duration of prior systemic therapy and presence of liver metastases; primary endpoint overall survival; interim futility analysis prespecified
RAS-005.population: Adults with metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma who had progressed on gemcitabine-based chemotherapy
RAS-005.n: 137 randomised; 55 and 57 evaluable with measurable disease in the experimental and control arms respectively
RAS-005.time_frame: Randomisation September 2012 - May 2014; follow-up to death or 3 years after registration
RAS-005.finding: Median OS 3.9 months with selumetinib + MK-2206 versus 6.7 months with mFOLFOX (HR 1.37, 95% CI 0.90-2.08, P=0.15; Fig 3). Median PFS 1.9 versus 2.0 months (HR 1.61, 95% CI 1.07-2.43, P=0.02; Fig 2). Partial responses 1 versus 5; stable disease 12 versus 14; no complete responses in either arm. Grade >=3 toxicity in 39 versus 23 patients. The futility boundary was crossed at interim analysis and results were released early.
RAS-005.effect: OS HR 1.37 (0.90-2.08) favouring chemotherapy; PFS HR 1.61 (1.07-2.43), P=0.02 favouring chemotherapy
RAS-005.limitations: Phase 2 size (one-sided alpha 0.10), not a definitive superiority test; no pharmacodynamic confirmation of target inhibition in tumour; toxicity caused more discontinuations in the experimental arm.
RAS-005.interpretation: Randomised comparison against active chemotherapy: directly excludes a clinically meaningful benefit of dual downstream (MEK + AKT) blockade in this setting and provides a contemporaneous mFOLFOX benchmark.

glosses.clinical-trials: A randomized phase 2 trial stopped at interim futility in which MEK plus AKT inhibition did worse than chemotherapy.
glosses.earlier-pathway-failures: The randomized SWOG S1115 trial of MEK plus AKT inhibition, stopped at interim futility with shorter survival than chemotherapy.

RAS-006.citation: Awad MM, Liu S, Rybkin II, Arbour KC, Dilly J, Zhu VW, et al. Acquired Resistance to KRAS(G12C) Inhibition in Cancer. N Engl J Med. 2021;384(25):2382-2393.
RAS-006.clinical_status: Descriptive human resistance study; no approved intervention follows directly from it. Checked 2026-10-08.
RAS-006.design: Paired pre-treatment versus post-progression genomic (tissue and/or cell-free DNA) and histologic analysis, plus a Ba/F3 positive-selection deep mutational scanning screen of nearly all single-amino-acid KRAS G12C variants
RAS-006.population: 38 patients with KRAS G12C-mutant cancers treated with adagrasib monotherapy: 27 NSCLC, 10 colorectal, 1 appendiceal (no pancreatic cases in this cohort)
RAS-006.n: 38 patients; 9 NSCLC with paired tissue biopsies; saturation mutagenesis library of KRAS G12C single substitutions
RAS-006.time_frame: At radiographic progression on adagrasib (phase 1/2 KRYSTAL-1 program)
RAS-006.finding: Putative resistance mechanisms detected in 17/38 patients (45%), of whom 7/38 (18%) had multiple coincident mechanisms. Acquired KRAS alterations: G12D/R/V/W, G13D, Q61H, R68S, H95D/Q/R, Y96C and high-level amplification of the KRAS G12C allele; secondary mutations inside the adagrasib-binding (switch-II) pocket in 4 patients (Y96C in 1 NSCLC, H95Q+H95R in 1 CRC, R68S+H95D in 1 NSCLC, H95R in 1 CRC). Acquired bypass mechanisms: MET amplification; activating mutations in NRAS, BRAF, MAP2K1 and RET; oncogenic fusions involving ALK, RET, BRAF, RAF1 and FGFR3; loss-of-function mutations in NF1 and PTEN. In 2 of 9 NSCLC patients with paired tissue, histologic transformation to squamous-cell carcinoma occurred with no other identified mechanism. The deep mutational scan systematically mapped the KRAS substitutions conferring resistance.
RAS-006.effect: 45% of patients with an identifiable genomic/histologic resistance mechanism; 18% polyclonal
RAS-006.limitations: No pancreatic patients; tissue available in a minority; mechanisms unidentified in 55% of patients.
RAS-006.interpretation: Paired within-patient design plus a saturating in vitro genetic screen: establishes that escape is polyclonal and convergent on restored RAS-MAPK signalling and defines which KRAS substitutions suffice.

glosses.ras-resistance: A study of 38 patients progressing on a KRAS G12C drug in lung and colorectal cancer, which found a resistance mechanism in 45% and secondary drug-binding-site mutations in four.

RAS-007.citation: Golan T, Khvalevsky EZ, Hubert A, Gabai RM, Hen N, Segal A, et al. RNAi therapy targeting KRAS in combination with chemotherapy for locally advanced pancreatic cancer patients. Oncotarget. 2015;6(27):24560-24570.
RAS-007.clinical_status: siG12D-LODER remains investigational; not approved in the US. Checked 2026-10-08.
RAS-007.design: Open-label phase 1/2a dose-escalation study of an intratumoral biodegradable implant releasing anti-KRAS G12D siRNA over ~4 months, combined with chemotherapy
RAS-007.population: Patients with non-operable locally advanced pancreatic cancer (LAPC), first-line setting
RAS-007.n: 15 patients enrolled and treated; 12 evaluable by CT; 10 with elevated baseline CA19-9
RAS-007.time_frame: 8-week safety follow-up; survival followed to death; implant releases siRNA over ~4 months
RAS-007.finding: Most frequent adverse events were grade 1-2 (89% of events); 5 patients had serious adverse events. Of 12 patients with CT assessment, none showed tumour progression; 10/12 had stable disease and 2/12 had a partial response. CA19-9 decreased in 7/10 (70%). Median overall survival 15.12 months; 18-month survival 38.5%.
RAS-007.effect: Median OS 15.12 months; 2/12 partial responses; no radiographic progression in evaluable patients
RAS-007.limitations: n=15; locally advanced (not metastatic) population; combined with two different chemotherapy backbones; no control arm; survival in LAPC is strongly influenced by patient selection.
RAS-007.interpretation: Early-phase single-arm safety study: shows feasibility and tolerability of local mutant-allele silencing but cannot separate the implant's effect from concurrent chemotherapy or from LAPC natural history.

RAS-008.citation: Xue JY, Zhao Y, Aronowitz J, Mai TT, Vides A, Qeriqi B, et al. Rapid non-uniform adaptation to conformation-specific KRAS(G12C) inhibition. Nature. 2020;577(7790):421-425.
RAS-008.clinical_status: Preclinical mechanism; underpins ongoing KRAS inhibitor + EGFR-antibody combination trials (approved only in colorectal cancer). Checked 2026-10-08.
RAS-008.design: Single-cell RNA sequencing trajectory analysis, live reporter (p27K- CDK-binding-defective) tracking, CRISPR sgRNA depletion screens, pharmacological rescue
RAS-008.population: Isogenic human KRAS G12C cancer cell lines (including pancreatic MIA PaCa-2 lineage) analysed at single-cell resolution; xenografts
RAS-008.n: Single-cell transcriptomes across treatment timepoints; reporter-based subpopulation quantification; multiple cell lines
RAS-008.time_frame: Hours to 72 h after treatment onset
RAS-008.finding: Shortly after G12C inhibitor treatment the isogenic population split into two fates: ~80% of cells entered a transcriptionally distinct quiescent G0 state with high p27K- reporter and low KRAS output, while ~20% were p27K--low rapidly adapting cells with higher active KRAS that progressed past the G1 restriction point (Fig 1f-j; Extended Data Figs 4-5). Bimodality was specific to the G12C inhibitor and not reproduced by MEK or ERK inhibitors (Extended Data Fig 5b-c). Adaptation required synthesis of new KRAS G12C protein which is kept in the active, drug-insensitive (GTP-bound) state by EGFR and aurora kinase A signalling. HBEGF mRNA fell immediately after treatment then rebounded at 48-72 h, localised by single-cell analysis to a quiescent cell cluster, with an approximately 2-fold rise in secreted HBEGF protein (Extended Data Figs 6-7). sgRNAs targeting EGFR-signalling intermediates…
RAS-008.effect: ~80% quiescent versus ~20% rapidly adapting cells; ~2-fold increase in secreted HBEGF at 48-72 h
RAS-008.limitations: In vitro and xenograft only; the specific inhibitor is a tool compound; no human validation of the EGFR/aurora dependency in PDAC.
RAS-008.interpretation: Perturbation plus single-cell resolution: identifies a non-genetic, pre-existing-fate-independent mechanism of immediate drug tolerance and shows that blocking the adaptive inputs converts a partial response into a durable one in vitro.

glosses.growth-control: A cell and xenograft study showing cells adapt to KRAS G12C inhibitors within days by making fresh, receptor-activated KRAS.
glosses.kras: A cell and xenograft study showing adaptation to KRAS G12C inhibitors within days through receptor-driven fresh KRAS.
glosses.kras-g12c-inhibitors: A single-cell study showing that within days of inactive-state G12C inhibition about a fifth of cells, including a pancreatic line, resume growth by making new KRAS held active by EGFR and aurora kinase A.
glosses.ras-resistance: Laboratory work showing that within hours of KRAS G12C blockade about a fifth of cells resume growing by making fresh KRAS protein that receptor signaling keeps active.
glosses.earlier-pathway-failures: Laboratory work showing that cells resume growth within hours of KRAS G12C blockade by making new KRAS protein that receptor signaling keeps switched on.

RAS-009.citation: Li J, Zhao J, Cao B, Fang J, Li X, Wang M, et al. Efficacy and safety of glecirasib in solid tumors with KRAS G12C mutation: A pooled analysis of two phase I/II trials. Cancer Commun (Lond). 2025;45(11):1500-1512.
RAS-009.clinical_status: Glecirasib is not FDA-approved; it holds US orphan drug designation and, as reported in Janne et al. 2026, a breakthrough therapy designation in China for KRAS G12C pancreatic cancer. Checked 2026-10-08.
RAS-009.design: Prespecified pooled analysis of two open-label phase I/II trials with similar eligibility and endpoints but different recruitment regions; primary pooled endpoint objective response rate (RECIST v1.1, investigator-assessed with confirmation at >=4 weeks in NCT05009329)
RAS-009.population: Adults with KRAS G12C-mutant solid tumours excluding NSCLC and CRC; 24/54 had >=2 prior lines; largest subgroup pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
RAS-009.n: 54 treated (32 PDAC, 8 biliary tract, 4 small intestinal, 3 gastric, 2 appendiceal, 5 other); 53 efficacy-evaluable; 32 PDAC efficacy-evaluable
RAS-009.time_frame: Data cutoff 30 June 2024; median follow-up 14.6 months for PDAC and 16.8 months for other tumours
RAS-009.finding: Pooled confirmed ORR 27/53 = 50.9% (95% CI 36.8-64.9). PDAC: confirmed ORR 46.9% (95% CI 29.1-65.3) of 32 patients; median time to response 2.6 months (range 1.3-8.1); median PFS 5.5 months (95% CI 4.2-9.8); median OS 10.8 months (95% CI 8.9-12.5) (Table 3; Fig 2). Other tumours (n=21): ORR 71.4% (5/7) biliary tract, 100% (4/4) small intestine, 66.7% (2/3) gastric; median PFS 6.9 months (95% CI 5.5-NE); median OS 14.4 months (95% CI 6.9-NE). TP53 was co-mutated in 17/20 (85%) of sequenced PDAC cases with no difference in ORR by TP53, CDKN2A or ARID1A co-alteration status (Supplementary Fig S1B-D); baseline KRAS G12C variant allele frequency was not associated with efficacy. The authors tabulate the comparison with CodeBreaK 100 (ORR 21.1%, PFS 4.0, OS 6.9 months in 38 patients) and KRYSTAL-1 PDAC (ORR 33.3%, PFS 5.4, OS 8.0 months in 21 patients).
RAS-009.effect: PDAC ORR 46.9% (29.1-65.3); median PFS 5.5 mo; median OS 10.8 mo
RAS-009.limitations: Single-arm pooled analysis; response assessment not centrally reviewed; cross-trial comparison with CodeBreaK 100/KRYSTAL-1 is not randomised; median OS of 10.8 months still indicates progression within about half a year.
RAS-009.interpretation: Independent replication at the same molecular target with a different agent and population: distinguishes 'pancreas is refractory' from 'drug-level differences', though without randomisation.

glosses.kras-alleles-wildtype: A pooled analysis of glecirasib in which 46.9 percent of 32 KRAS G12C pancreatic patients responded.
glosses.kras-g12c-inhibitors: A pooled analysis of two phase 1/2 trials of glecirasib, in which 47 percent of 32 patients with KRAS G12C pancreatic cancer responded by investigator assessment.

RAS-010.citation: Dilly J, Hoffman MT, Abbassi L, Li Z, Paradiso F, Parent BD, et al. Mechanisms of Resistance to Oncogenic KRAS Inhibition in Pancreatic Cancer. Cancer Discov. 2024;14(11):2135-2161.
RAS-010.clinical_status: Mechanistic/translational; motivates combination trials. No approved combination follows from it as of 2026-10-08.
RAS-010.design: Multi-level study: paired clinical ctDNA sequencing and ddPCR, low-pass whole-genome sequencing of cell-free DNA, PRISM/cell-line and organoid drug sensitivity with transcriptomics and immunoblotting, long-term in vivo KRAS G12D inhibition with molecular characterisation at relapse, plus an…
RAS-010.population: 22 patients with KRAS G12C-mutant PDAC treated with adagrasib (patients 1-8) or sotorasib (patients 9-22) with paired pre-treatment and end-of-treatment ctDNA; plus PDAC cell lines, patient-derived organoids (PDO), PDX and the autochthonous KPC mouse model
RAS-010.n: 22 PDAC patients (clinical); aggregated resistance cohort across NSCLC, CRC, PDAC and other GI cancers; multiple cell lines, PDOs, PDX and KPC mice
RAS-010.time_frame: Clinical samples at progression; in vivo long-term dosing to relapse
RAS-010.finding: Putative genetic mechanisms of primary or acquired resistance were identified in 9/22 (41%) PDAC patients (Fig 1A-C). Among 4 patients with progressive disease: high-level MYC amplification (patient 1); concurrent gains/amplification of KRAS G12C, BRAF, ERBB2 and CDK4 (patient 9); rising variant allele frequency of a pre-existing subclonal KRAS G12R (patient 11). Treatment-emergent alterations at acquired resistance included KRAS G12C amplification/gain (patients 6, 9, 13, 22), EGFR amplification/gain (patients 2, 13), activating PIK3CA mutations (patients 13, 22), an oncogenic NFE2L2 D29H variant (patient 21) and a treatment-emergent KRAS A146P (patient 21); patient 4 showed high-level amplifications of ERBB2, MET, CDK6, MYC and ABCB1 on low-pass WGS of cfDNA. No drug-binding-site (switch-II) mutations were observed in the PDAC cohort. In the aggregated cross-cancer cohort, putative…
RAS-010.effect: 41% of PDAC patients with an identifiable genetic mechanism; 54% of PDAC with none; cross-cancer treatment-emergent KRAS alterations 29% in PDAC versus 41% in CRC
RAS-010.limitations: 22 patients is small and partly overlaps in trial provenance with the cohorts in RAS-001/RAS-002; most resistance mechanisms remain correlative; the in vivo work uses a G12D inhibitor whose human trial was later terminated.
RAS-010.interpretation: Cross-scale triangulation: patient ctDNA defines what emerges, isogenic/organoid models test whether candidate lesions are sufficient, and the autochthonous model shows the time course from deep regression to relapse.

glosses.daraxonrasib: A study of 22 pancreatic patients progressing on KRAS G12C inhibitors, in which no genetic resistance mechanism was found in about half.
glosses.kras-g12c-inhibitors: A resistance study of 22 pancreatic patients treated with adagrasib or sotorasib, in which a genetic cause of resistance was found in 41 percent and none in 54 percent.
glosses.ras-resistance: An analysis of 22 patients with KRAS G12C pancreatic cancer in which 41% had an identifiable genetic cause of resistance, none involving the drug-binding site.

RAS-011.citation: Jiang J, Jiang L, Maldonato BJ, Wang Y, Holderfield M, Aronchik I, et al. Translational and Therapeutic Evaluation of RAS-GTP Inhibition by RMC-6236 in RAS-Driven Cancers. Cancer Discov. 2024;14(6):994-1017.
RAS-011.clinical_status: RMC-6236/daraxonrasib (RASONQUE) was subsequently FDA-approved for metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma on 26 August 2026. Checked 2026-10-08.
RAS-011.design: Discovery pharmacology plus translational PK/PD and PK/efficacy modelling used to predict clinically active human doses, with two illustrative clinical case studies
RAS-011.population: Human cancer cell-line panels (PRISM), KRAS G12X cell-line-derived xenografts including the pancreatic Capan-2 model, and two patients treated on the phase 1/1b trial (one KRAS G12X NSCLC, one KRAS G12X pancreatic adenocarcinoma)
RAS-011.n: Cell-line panel; multi-model in vivo 'mouse clinical trial'; 2 patient case studies
RAS-011.time_frame: Preclinical dosing over weeks; clinical case studies within the ongoing phase 1/1b (NCT05379985, first posted 2022-05-18)
RAS-011.finding: RMC-6236 showed potent anticancer activity across RAS-addicted cell lines, most strongly those with KRAS codon-12 mutations; neither cyclophilin A (PPIA) mRNA expression nor KRAS mutant/wild-type allele copy number significantly affected sensitivity in PRISM (Supplementary Fig S1H-J). Dose-dependent blood and tumour exposure were observed in the Capan-2 pancreatic xenograft after single doses of 3, 10 or 25 mg/kg (Fig 2A). Oral dosing was tolerated and drove profound tumour regressions across tumour types in a KRAS G12X xenograft mouse clinical trial. Translational PK/efficacy and PK/PD modelling predicted that 100 mg daily would achieve tumour control and 300 mg daily would achieve objective responses in patients; consistent with this, objective responses were observed in two patients treated at 300 mg daily with advanced KRAS G12X lung and pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
RAS-011.effect: Model-predicted 300 mg daily for objective response; 2/2 illustrative patients responded
RAS-011.limitations: Industry-sponsored discovery paper; the clinical component is two case studies with no denominator; cyclophilin-A dependence of the tri-complex mechanism is assessed only by mRNA.
RAS-011.interpretation: Quantitative exposure-response modelling: links target coverage to tumour effect and makes a falsifiable dose prediction that the trial then tested; the two cases are anecdotal, not inferential.

glosses.daraxonrasib: The translational study that modeled the daraxonrasib dose and reported the first two patient responses at 300 mg daily.
glosses.ras-on-inhibitors: The translational paper that modeled a human dose of daraxonrasib from mouse exposure-response data and reported responses in the first two patients treated at 300 mg daily.

RAS-012.citation: Aronchik I, Kar S, Zhuang Y, Ahler E, Lai LP, Seshadri V, et al. Acquired resistance to the RAS(ON) multi-selective inhibitor daraxonrasib guides rational combination therapy strategies in pancreatic cancer. Nat Med. 2026;32(8):2865-2877.
RAS-012.clinical_status: Resistance analysis supporting the RASolute combination programme; daraxonrasib monotherapy is US-approved for mPDAC (26 August 2026); none of the tested combinations is approved. Checked 2026-10-08.
RAS-012.design: Paired within-patient targeted ctDNA sequencing of >800 genes at baseline and progression, followed by engineered gain-of-function models and isolation of resistant clones under sustained in vivo drug pressure, then combination testing
RAS-012.population: 44 patients with RAS-mutant metastatic PDAC treated with daraxonrasib monotherapy (300 mg once daily) in the phase 1/2 trial, with paired pre-treatment and end-of-treatment ctDNA; plus human and murine PDAC cell lines, organoids, CDX and PDX models
RAS-012.n: 44 patients with paired ctDNA; multiple engineered and resistant-clone models (HPAF-II, HPAC, KP-4, HuP-T3, AP009 murine organoids)
RAS-012.time_frame: Paired sampling at baseline and at progression on monotherapy; preclinical long-term dosing to relapse
RAS-012.finding: Acquired alterations were detected in ctDNA from 11/44 patients (25%). Acquired alterations in RAF genes occurred in 5/44 (11%), comprising single-nucleotide ARAF, BRAF and RAF1 variants, with co-occurring mutant KRAS amplification in one patient (patient 11). RTK alterations occurred in 4/44 (9%), including an ERBB2 (HER2) amplification (copy number 2.31) and a MET gene fusion, each co-occurring with mutant KRAS amplification (Fig 1a-b). No secondary KRAS mutations were found in any preclinical PDAC model with acquired resistance to long-term RAS(ON) inhibition, in vitro or in vivo. Concordant mechanisms were found or mechanistically established in models, including mutant KRAS and MYC amplification and RTK upregulation. In HPAF-II tumours (which carry baseline KRAS amplification) RMC-7977 drove initial regressions with relapse after long-term dosing, and outgrowing tumours showed…
RAS-012.effect: 25% (11/44) of patients with an identified acquired genomic mechanism; RAF 11%; RTK 9%
RAS-012.limitations: Industry (Revolution Medicines) analysis of its own trial; ctDNA-only (no tissue) for the clinical component; combination benefit shown only in mice; shares participants with the phase 1/2 report (RAS-032), so only this record counts toward the minimum for that family.
RAS-012.interpretation: Paired human sampling plus engineered sufficiency tests in matched models: supports convergent RAS-pathway reactivation as the dominant escape route and identifies which combinations prevent it in a preparation.

glosses.kras: A blood-DNA analysis of 44 patients progressing on daraxonrasib, finding RAF, receptor or KRAS-amplification changes in a quarter.
glosses.genome-evolution: A blood-DNA analysis of 44 patients progressing on daraxonrasib, finding RAF, receptor or KRAS-amplification changes in a quarter.
glosses.ctdna: Paired ctDNA sequencing before and after daraxonrasib treatment identifying the alterations that drove resistance.
glosses.daraxonrasib: A paired blood-DNA analysis of 44 patients progressing on daraxonrasib, finding acquired RAF, receptor or KRAS-copy changes in a quarter and no binding-site mutations.
glosses.ras-on-inhibitors: A circulating-tumor-DNA analysis of 44 patients progressing on daraxonrasib, in which an acquired genetic cause was found in 25 percent, mostly RAF and receptor changes.
glosses.ras-resistance: The manufacturer's analysis of blood DNA from 44 patients progressing on daraxonrasib, which found an acquired genetic change in a quarter of them.

RAS-013.citation: Bandi DSR, Nagaraju GP, Sarvesh S, Carstens JL, Foote JB, Graff EC, et al. ADT-1004: a first-in-class, oral pan-RAS inhibitor with robust antitumor activity in preclinical models of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. Mol Cancer. 2025;24(1):76.
RAS-013.clinical_status: Preclinical; ADT-1004 is not in a reported clinical trial for PDAC as of 2026-10-08.
RAS-013.design: Preclinical intervention study with target-engagement pharmacodynamics, allele-spanning PDX panel, resistance-model arms and a wild-type selectivity arm; immune profiling of the tumour microenvironment
RAS-013.population: Orthotopic murine KRAS G12D PDAC (KPC-luc, 2838c3-luc) in immunocompetent C57BL/6J mice; four KRAS-mutant PDAC patient-derived xenografts subcutaneously in NSG mice; parental and inhibitor-resistant MIA PaCa-2 (KRAS G12C) and MRTX1133-resistant KRAS G12D cells; RAS wild-type BxPC-3 as a…
RAS-013.n: Two orthotopic syngeneic models, four KRAS-mutant PDX models, resistant and parental cell-derived tumours, one RAS wild-type model
RAS-013.time_frame: Weeks of oral dosing per model
RAS-013.finding: ADT-1004 potently blocked tumour growth and RAS activation in the murine orthotopic PDAC models without discernible toxicity, with target engagement shown as reduced activated RAS and reduced ERK phosphorylation. It suppressed tumour growth in PDX models bearing KRAS G12D, G12V, G12C or G13Q mutations, and increased intratumoral CD4+ and CD8+ T cells together with MHCII+ M1-like macrophages and dendritic cells. ADT-1004 showed superior efficacy compared with sotorasib and adagrasib in tumour models rendered resistant to those KRAS G12C inhibitors, and compared with MRTX1133 in MRTX1133-resistant KRAS G12D mutant cells. It did not affect growth of tumours formed from RAS wild-type BxPC-3 cells, indicating mutant-RAS selectivity.
RAS-013.effect: Growth suppression across four KRAS alleles; superiority over allele-selective inhibitors in matched resistant models; no effect in RAS wild-type tumours
RAS-013.limitations: Preclinical only; ADT-1004 has no reported human data; immune profiling is descriptive without depletion controls; single laboratory.
RAS-013.interpretation: Independent chemotype with a built-in selectivity control (RAS wild-type model) and resistance-model arms: supports that broad mutant-RAS inhibition, rather than a particular scaffold, is what overcomes allele-selective resistance.

RAS-014.citation: Zhao Y, Murciano-Goroff YR, Xue JY, Ang A, Lucas J, Mai TT, et al. Diverse alterations associated with resistance to KRAS(G12C) inhibition. Nature. 2021;599(7886):679-683.
RAS-014.clinical_status: Descriptive human resistance study with preclinical combination rationale; no approved ERK-inhibitor combination exists. Checked 2026-10-08.
RAS-014.design: Paired clinical liquid and/or tissue biopsy sequencing, PDX/cell-line resistance modelling, single-cell sequencing of an isogenic resistant lineage, and genetic/pharmacological co-targeting of ERK-signalling intermediates
RAS-014.population: 43 patients treated with sotorasib (36 NSCLC, 3 colorectal, 4 other cancers including one pancreatic, one melanoma, one small cell lung and one spindle cell carcinoma); matched pre- and post-treatment specimens; PDX and cell-line models
RAS-014.n: 43 patients (27 with treatment-emergent alterations); multiple PDX and cell-line models; single-cell analysis of one isogenic lineage
RAS-014.time_frame: At progression on sotorasib; model experiments over weeks
RAS-014.finding: Treatment-emergent alterations were observed across 27 of 43 patients, including alterations in KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, EGFR, FGFR2, MYC and other genes. In PDX and cell-line models, resistance was associated with low-allele-frequency hotspot mutations in KRAS (G12V or G13D), NRAS (Q61K or G13R), MRAS (Q71R) and/or BRAF (G596R), mirroring the patient observations. Single-cell sequencing of an isogenic lineage identified secondary RAS and/or BRAF mutations within the same cells that carried KRAS G12C, where they bypassed inhibition without affecting target inactivation. Genetic or pharmacological targeting of ERK-signalling intermediates enhanced the antiproliferative effect of G12C inhibitor treatment in models with acquired RAS or BRAF mutations. The authors note the clinical baseline for comparison: sotorasib gives a 30-40% response rate and roughly 6-month median PFS in lung cancer, and…
RAS-014.effect: Treatment-emergent alterations in 27/43 patients; minor subclones sufficient to bypass inhibition
RAS-014.limitations: Only one pancreatic patient; most of the cohort is NSCLC; no formal frequency estimates per tumour type.
RAS-014.interpretation: Independent replication plus single-cell clonal resolution: distinguishes 'target not engaged' from 'target engaged but bypassed', which is the central distinction for the atlas's subject-specific check.

glosses.daraxonrasib: A study of 43 patients across cancer types in which diverse genetic alterations emerged at resistance to KRAS G12C inhibition, only one of them pancreatic.
glosses.ras-resistance: A study of 43 patients on a KRAS G12C drug, mostly lung cancer, showing that secondary RAS and RAF mutations arise inside the same cells and bypass the drug without displacing it.

RAS-015.citation: Tanaka N, Lin JJ, Li C, Ryan MB, Zhang J, Kiedrowski LA, et al. Clinical Acquired Resistance to KRAS(G12C) Inhibition through a Novel KRAS Switch-II Pocket Mutation and Polyclonal Alterations Converging on RAS-MAPK Reactivation. Cancer Discov. 2021;11(8):1913-1922.
RAS-015.clinical_status: Mechanistic precedent for the tri-complex RAS(ON) class now represented clinically by elironrasib, zoldonrasib and daraxonrasib. Checked 2026-10-08.
RAS-015.design: Serial cell-free DNA analysis in a single patient (N-of-1 natural experiment), structural modelling, and in vitro functional testing of the identified mutation against multiple inhibitors including a tri-complex active-state inhibitor
RAS-015.population: One 67-year-old woman with metastatic KRAS G12C-mutant NSCLC treated on the dose-expansion cohort of the phase 1 adagrasib study; engineered and patient-derived KRAS G12C cancer models
RAS-015.n: 1 patient with serial cfDNA; engineered and patient-derived model systems
RAS-015.time_frame: Response then progression within ~4 months; serial cfDNA across treatment
RAS-015.finding: Initial scans showed a 32% reduction in tumour size by RECIST v1.1, with progression after approximately 4 months. Serial cfDNA identified 10 heterogeneous resistance alterations spanning four genes (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MAP2K1), all converging on reactivation of RAS-MAPK signalling. A novel KRAS Y96D mutation affecting the switch-II pocket - the binding site of adagrasib and other inactive-state inhibitors - was identified; structural modelling showed it interferes with key protein-drug interactions, and it conferred resistance to these inhibitors in engineered and patient-derived KRAS G12C models. The functionally distinct tri-complex active-state inhibitor RM-018 retained the ability to bind and inhibit KRAS G12C/Y96D and overcame resistance. The authors note that mutations affecting Y96 appear to be a shared vulnerability for the available inactive-state G12C inhibitors.
RAS-015.effect: 32% initial tumour reduction then progression at ~4 months; 10 convergent resistance alterations; RM-018 retains activity against G12C/Y96D
RAS-015.limitations: N=1, NSCLC not PDAC; RM-018 is a tool compound; same parent trial as RAS-006 (different reported patient, but overlap cannot be fully excluded).
RAS-015.interpretation: N-of-1 with molecular time course plus an in vitro rescue: the drug-class switch is a discriminating test that distinguishes a binding-site problem from a pathway problem.

glosses.ctdna: A case in which serial plasma sequencing identified ten resistance mutations emerging during KRAS G12C inhibitor treatment.
glosses.kras-g12c-inhibitors: A single lung cancer patient whose tumor acquired a switch-II pocket mutation that defeated inactive-state G12C inhibitors but not an ON-state tri-complex compound.
glosses.ras-resistance: A single-patient report in lung cancer in which a new mutation in the drug's binding pocket caused progression after an initial 32% tumor reduction.

RAS-016.citation: Bryant KL, Stalnecker CA, Zeitouni D, Klomp JE, Peng S, Tikunov AP, et al. Combination of ERK and autophagy inhibition as a treatment approach for pancreatic cancer. Nat Med. 2019;25(4):628-640.
RAS-016.clinical_status: Preclinical rationale; hydroxychloroquine plus chemotherapy has been tested clinically in PDAC with limited benefit, and no ERK-inhibitor-plus-autophagy-inhibitor regimen is approved. Checked 2026-10-08.
RAS-016.design: Perturbation study: KRAS suppression and pharmacological ERK/MEK inhibition with quantitative autophagic-flux reporters, synergy analysis (Chou-Talalay and Bliss), then in vivo combination testing
RAS-016.population: Human KRAS-mutant PDAC cell lines (8 lines with autophagy reporters), three-dimensional organoid cultures, and two heterogeneous KRAS-mutant patient-derived xenograft models
RAS-016.n: 8 human PDAC lines for flux; organoids; 2 PDX models in vivo
RAS-016.time_frame: 24 h flux assays; weeks of in vivo dosing
RAS-016.finding: Short-term (24 h) ERK inhibition stimulated a 3- to 30-fold increase in autophagy in 8 of 8 human PDAC cell lines carrying the mCherry-EGFP-LC3B reporter (Fig 2a-b), confirmed by a 2- to 12-fold increase in EGFP+ autophagosomes in a complementary reporter. Concurrent treatment with SCH772984, ulixertinib or binimetinib synergistically enhanced chloroquine-mediated growth inhibition, with combination index values <1 across a broad concentration range (Fig 5a-c), and synergy was maintained in three-dimensional organoid cultures (Fig 5e-f). In two KRAS-mutant PDAC PDX models, ERK inhibitor alone significantly slowed tumour growth, but the ERK inhibitor plus hydroxychloroquine combination blocked tumour progression and extended survival more effectively, with significantly smaller harvested tumours than ERK inhibitor alone (Fig 5g-h). The authors note that hydroxychloroquine monotherapy…
RAS-016.effect: 3-30-fold induction of autophagic flux in 8/8 lines; combination index <1; blocked PDX progression versus single agent
RAS-016.limitations: Preclinical; achievable human hydroxychloroquine exposures may not reach the concentrations used; ERK inhibitors have their own dose-limiting toxicity; no immunocompetent model.
RAS-016.interpretation: Induced-dependency logic tested by two mechanistically distinct autophagy blocks and three distinct pathway inhibitors: supports that the dependency is created by pathway inhibition rather than being constitutive.

glosses.nutrient-scavenging: A study showing that inhibiting ERK or MEK raises autophagy three- to thirtyfold in pancreatic cancer cells, making the two blocks synergistic in organoids and patient-derived xenografts.

RAS-017.citation: Kinsey CG, Camolotto SA, Boespflug AM, Guillen KP, Foth M, Truong A, et al. Protective autophagy elicited by RAF-MEK-ERK inhibition suggests a treatment strategy for RAS-driven cancers. Nat Med. 2019;25(4):620-627.
RAS-017.clinical_status: Preclinical with an anecdotal clinical response; no MEK-plus-autophagy-inhibitor regimen is approved for PDAC. Checked 2026-10-08.
RAS-017.design: Perturbation study combining pharmacological MEK inhibition with either chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine or a tetracycline-inducible dominant-negative ATG4B (ATG4B C74A) genetic autophagy block; plus a single compassionate-use clinical observation
RAS-017.population: Human PDAC cell lines (MIA PaCa-2, BxPC3) and xenografts in NOD/SCID mice; patient-derived xenografts of NRAS-mutant melanoma and BRAF-mutant colorectal cancer; one patient with PDAC
RAS-017.n: Multiple cell lines and xenograft cohorts; cross-tumour PDX panel; 1 patient
RAS-017.time_frame: Weeks of in vivo dosing; single-patient clinical course
RAS-017.finding: Inhibition of KRAS-RAF-MEK-ERK signalling increased autophagic flux in PDAC cells. Dominant-negative ATG4B combined with trametinib promoted regression of established MIA PaCa-2 xenografts in a tumour-cell-autonomous manner (Fig 3d), showing that genetic autophagy blockade reproduces the chloroquine effect. Trametinib plus chloroquine or hydroxychloroquine promoted regression in MIA PaCa-2 and BxPC3 xenografts and in patient-derived xenografts of NRAS-mutant melanoma and BRAF-mutant colorectal cancer, indicating the effect is not restricted to PDAC. Treatment of one PDAC patient with trametinib plus hydroxychloroquine resulted in a partial but, in the authors' words, striking disease response.
RAS-017.effect: Xenograft regression with genetic autophagy block plus trametinib; one patient partial response
RAS-017.limitations: N-of-1 clinical observation; immunodeficient hosts; trametinib monotherapy had already failed in a randomised PDAC trial, so the clinical premise rests on the combination.
RAS-017.interpretation: Genetic loss-of-function control for a pharmacological finding: raises confidence that the induced dependency is autophagy itself, not an off-target chloroquine effect. The single patient is anecdotal.

glosses.nutrient-scavenging: A companion study using a genetic autophagy block alongside a MEK inhibitor to show the synergy is attributable to autophagy rather than to off-target effects of chloroquine.

RAS-018.citation: Janne PA, Doi T, Garrido-Laguna I, Hollebecque A, Bando H, Juergens RA, et al. The SOS1 Inhibitor BI 1701963 as Monotherapy or in Combination with Trametinib in Patients with KRAS Mutation-Positive Solid Tumors: Results from Phase I Trials. Clin Cancer Res. 2026;32(15):3135-3145.
RAS-018.clinical_status: Negative phase I; BI 1701963 development for this indication did not progress to a positive phase II signal and no SOS1 inhibitor is approved in the US. Checked 2026-10-08.
RAS-018.design: Phase I dose escalation (part A) and confirmation (part B) with maximum tolerated dose / recommended phase II dose as primary objectives and preliminary efficacy as a secondary objective
RAS-018.population: Patients with previously treated, relapsed/refractory, KRAS mutation-positive advanced or metastatic solid tumours; monotherapy cohort pooled from three trials and a combination cohort from one; most had received >=2 prior lines
RAS-018.n: 75 patients received BI 1701963 monotherapy (NCT04111458 n=52; NCT04835714 n=8 in Japan; NCT04627142 n=15 in China) and 19 received BI 1701963 plus trametinib (NCT04111458). Pancreatic cancer…
RAS-018.time_frame: Phase I dose escalation and confirmation across three registered trials; first-cycle fatal toxicity
